topics.title: [inference] Stage the shared vLLM 0.30 GPU candidate
topics.body:
Stage the immutable vLLM 0.30 candidate for H100 and GB200 with Torch 2.14.1 and CUDA 13.2. Both wheels come from shared fork source `47b411d5785d1c3dee0328334472d70310c53feb`. The normal Marin installer uses the candidate's architecture-specific dependency constraints and matching NVCC, CCCL and NVRTC components.

Add size-one `expert` and `context` dimensions to the Levanter serving mesh. Snowball's weight layout requires these names; their absence failed scoring after the model loaded. The dimensions preserve the existing data and tensor-parallel sizes. The numerical CPU regression reproduces the failure before the fix, then compares logits from the same weights on the canonical Snowball training mesh and the serving mesh.

Snowball's 64 representative cases passed on 8 H100s with Levanter and on 8 and 16 H100s with vLLM. The unchanged bounds on absolute token-probability differences are 0.075 for Levanter and 0.125 for vLLM. The largest logged differences were 0.056754, 0.059786 and 0.055632, respectively. The normal installer and a transport smoke check of brokered Qwen3-0.6B completions also passed on one H100. These results cover Marin's standalone Transformers 5.18 profile.

Snowball and Hero passed fresh training, checkpoint restoration and HF export on H100 and GB200 in MarinSkyRL's combined training and serving profile (Transformers 5.12.1). Hero/GB200's driver finished successfully before a worker pod was deleted during shutdown; four queued worker retries for that completed run were canceled.

On matched inputs at batch 128 and context 4096, Hero's GB200 policy-update benchmark took 56.37 seconds with the refreshed [dependency profile](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/c9def79c0ac7d043879c669722aab311532b3b03/uv.lock) (Torch 2.14.1) versus 48.10 seconds with the shipping [dependency profile](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/f85737fc366d1f077ce9216b179a2a98a0bf8d14/uv.lock) (Torch 2.13.0), 17.2% longer. Peak GPU allocation was effectively unchanged. Several dependencies differ between these profiles; the cause remains unresolved. This performance regression is unaccepted.

Keep this draft pending official release qualification and protected promotion. The pinned wheels are staged in [marin-vllm-gpu-staged-candidate-47b411d5785d](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-staged-candidate-47b411d5785d). Rollback is GPU release `marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac`, source `01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e`. The [paired TPU refresh](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10023) uses a separate dependency environment. The [admin promotion handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10022#issuecomment-6093743002) records the remaining release gates, source promotion order and rollback refs.

topics.title: [grug] Compute the MoE routing-weight gradient on the expert side
topics.body:
With QuACK's expert MLP, the ragged all-to-all MoE takes its routing-weight gradient from the expert MLP's own backward, so the backward needs neither the expert outputs nor their return transport, and the hero saves the routed output instead of recomputing the expert down projection, the return all-to-all and the combine. The step shortens by 4.12% (13.541 to 13.005 s against #9832, over 26 scored steps). Peak HBM rises to 125.4 GiB of the 143.75 GiB pool.

The backend chooses the gradient together with its expert MLP kernel; `moe_mlp` takes no option for it. QuACK's expert MLP (SM100, SiLU, QuACK installed) takes the expert-side gradient for bfloat16 and float32 tokens, which is the hero's configuration. The portable `ragged_dot` expert MLP takes the exact gradient, <dout, y> over the kept expert outputs: it keeps y anyway, so the expert-side gradient would save it only the returned [TK, H] buffer and the return transport. QuACK with float16 tokens takes the exact gradient too. The expert-side gradient is zero at a zero weight, and zero or inexact wherever |w * dout| falls below the cotangent dtype's smallest normal number: 2^-126 in bfloat16 and float32, which only output cotangents near underflow reach, and 2^-14 in float16, which ordinary magnitudes reach. The hero's routing weights are positive renormalized sigmoids and its cotangents bfloat16. Forward, dx, dW13 and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; the routing-weight gradient differs at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp) at nonzero weights.

The gradient with respect to the combine weight w[t,k] is dS[t,k] = <dout[t], y[t,k]>, the only backward consumer of the expert down projection's output y. Since dy = w * dout and dh = dy W2^T, the same value is rowsum(dh * h) / w, built from tensors the expert MLP backward already holds. One custom VJP from dispatch to combine returns s = <h, dh> per expert row, sends it back with one [C, 1] f32 all-to-all per chunk, and forms dS = s / w in f32; dropped and padded slots get 0 by selection. The backward's transports reuse the forward transfers' offsets, swapped, and on GPU its weighted output cotangents come from #9832's scatter kernel.

The saved routed output fits the 114 GiB remat budget that #9831 gives the carry offload; the backward needs ~105 GiB. With the backward's transports no longer ordered after the recompute's, several collectives in flight gave run-to-run different gradients or hung on GB200, so every ragged run forces a collective overlap limit of 1.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0), each head compiled fresh.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [eval] Run each evaluation as a StepSpec
topics.body:
Run each selected evaluation as its own StepSpec. StepRunner owns locking, retries, and success caching at each result path. An Iris restart skips successful steps before starting their model servers. Each step starts its candidate and optional judge server; `--max-concurrent` bounds simultaneous evaluations (default 8). A server startup failure writes a failed record only for the affected evaluation.

The eval launcher binds StepSpecs when it submits a prepared batch, after caller changes to priority or executor. Each submission gets fresh run IDs, including AIME repeats. Step identities include the resolved model and evaluator configuration, runtime revisions, judge configuration, and policy version. Verified policy versions retain their pinned benchmark sources and Harbor/Evalchemy commits.

EvalDash reads the StepSpec status file in each run's record directory. It withholds scores from running or failed steps while showing those states in run views. Shared measurement extraction reads record contents without depending on dashboard enrichment. Historical records without a step status retain their existing display.

A crash after writing a record but before StepRunner marks the step successful can rerun that evaluation. The [October 6, 2026 incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/627) showed a successful record replaced after a duplicate eval was cancelled.

The safe affected repository suite (`uv run --no-project infra/ci/run_tests.py`) passed 2,390 tests, with 3 skipped and 5 expected failures. Another 95 EvalDash tests passed. The four Docker-backed EvalDash kernel tests were not run here; their local PostgreSQL fixture timed out in an earlier attempt.

topics.title: [inference] Start serve readiness timeout after placement
topics.body:
Start the serve readiness timeout when a task's current attempt has an assigned Iris worker or a node-bound Kubernetes pod, or when the task is running. Kubernetes reports Kueue-gated Pending pods as BUILDING; the previous state-count check treated them as placed and failed evaluations after 2,400 seconds without allocating a GPU. Federated task status can also show a peer display label as its worker ID before placement, so the waiter uses the current attempt's assignment.

Queued time remains subject to the four-hour placement deadline. Requeued attempts stop consuming the startup budget, and old attempts' placement details do not mark the new attempt as placed.

Fixes #10036

topics.title: Validate localized online feedback for tool-use failures
topics.body:
Design, implement, execute, and validate online feedback loops that target specific model failures at the smallest justified token or action span. Start with tool-call closure: after a complete valid payload, prefer a harness-accepted closing sequence over an observed invalid continuation. An open but still-valid prefix is not a failure.

The BFCL recovery campaign's extended DPO run fell from 34/123 successful Pi trials to 0/123 after eight updates. Whole-trajectory preferences did not preserve tool behavior. [Public analysis and artifacts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/tree/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b).

Reuse the online final-token preference optimization (FTPO) path in [MarinSkyRL #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887) where appropriate. [Dr. Doom](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691) demonstrated reduced repetitive tails, but its alternative-token selection does not verify tool repairs. FTPO already supplies exact-token candidates, a selected-position preference objective, frozen-reference logit regularization, and empty-window optimizer skipping. Its supported topology excludes TP>1, context parallelism, sequence parallelism, and packing.

Done when:

- Define separate failure predicates and positive-evidence requirements for closure, argument repair, repeated-error recovery, and eventual progress/finalization. Implement and validate closure first; mark the other behaviors as separate subsequent experiments rather than blending them into one reward.
- Preserve the exact conditioning tokens, harness/tool schema, model version, and verification evidence. A positive candidate must be valid under the same prefix. Admit verified candidates outside rollout top-K; support a short span when a delimiter is multi-token.
- Connect on-policy generation, target construction, actual optimizer updates, weight synchronization, and fresh generation in MarinSkyRL. Reuse existing roles/checkpointing; no critic or learned reward model is required for parser-verifiable cases.
- Run a Pi-only smoke and a bounded learning experiment on training-complement tasks. Compare local preference learning with positive-only masked SFT on the same repairs and an unchanged-model control. Record skipped versus applied updates and compute costs.
- Evaluate held-out protocol validity, accepted/executed calls, premature closure, repetition, and task solve rate before and after training. Evaluate other harnesses to measure transfer; do not infer transfer from Pi alone. Keep BFCL-Parity out of mined training targets.
- Publish pinned configuration, provenance, failure examples cleared for redistribution, and results including regressions. State that token-local supervision changes shared model weights and does not guarantee globally local effects or one-token compute cost.

[Campaign closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040); related work: [datakit local-pair mining #10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042) and [online multi-harness integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041). [Detailed proposed interventions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-repair-versus-online-rl-20261011.md).

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The BFCL campaign's native DPO initializer scored 34/123 on Pi, then 0/123 after eight updates; the [closeout](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040) attributes no proven mechanism to the collapse. The pinned October code configures required trajectory retention and native DPO with recurring Pi evaluation, but its older online launcher disables inline evaluation and starts from a recovery export rather than the audited final initializer. [MarinSkyRL FTPO #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887) supplies a selected-position objective for repetition; it has not verified tool-call repairs. This is an experiment and integration task, not a small isolated fix; [#10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041) owns the general online loop and [#10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042) owns offline pair mining.

**Relevant code**
- [`collect.py#L93-L175`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/collect.py#L93-L175) — Pi trace and token retention.
- [`launch.py#L68-L145`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/launch.py#L68-L145) — older online recipe and disabled evaluation.
- [`final_dpo.py#L94-L220`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/final_dpo.py#L94-L220) — initializer, DPO, and Pi evaluation wiring.
- [`data.py#L48-L69`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/data.py#L48-L69) — audited complement/parity split.

# Localized online closure proposal

## Design

1. Define four separate predicates and evidence levels: closure after a complete valid tool payload, argument repair, repeated-error recovery, and eventual progress/finalization. Implement closure first. Mark the other three as later experiments with their own verified positives; do not pool them into a closure reward. An open, still-valid prefix and an infrastructure failure produce no target.
2. For each Pi closure target, retain the exact model-visible token prefix, generation boundary, tokenizer/model revision, tool schema, harness/runtime pins, task identity, and parser/execution receipt. Choose the shortest harness-accepted closing sequence for that *same* prefix only after a complete valid payload. Reject the observed continuation at the earliest transition that makes the call invalid. Verify the chosen sequence with the Pi parser and actual harness acceptance; parser validity alone is a weaker evidence level. Score verified candidates even when outside rollout top-K, and allow a bounded multi-token span for split delimiters. Keep BFCL-Parity identities out of targets.
3. Reuse MarinSkyRL #887's selected-position preference and frozen-reference logit regularization, extending candidate scoring and span masks only where closure requires them. Build targets from fresh Pi rollouts and connect them to non-skipped optimizer updates, weight publication, and new rollouts from the updated policy. Reuse the checkpoint/export and Pi evaluation path in `final_dpo.py`, and coordinate shared runtime work with [#10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041) and the open [TaskSession PR #9911](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9911). Keep TP=1, CP=1, sequence parallelism=1, and packing disabled until FTPO supports other topologies.
4. Run a Pi-only two-update smoke, then an at-most-eight-update pilot on the audited 3,518-task complement. Evaluate at initialization and after updates 2, 4, and 8; stop early for invalid-target admission, missing synchronization, or a marked held-out regression. Compare local preference training, positive-only masked SFT on the same verified repairs, and an unchanged initializer under matched task and evaluation conditions. Report eligible versus excluded targets, applied versus skipped updates, policy versions, GPU-hours, and any difference in training exposure.

## Validation and risks

Unit checks should reject incomplete-but-valid prefixes, changed token histories or schemas, BFCL-Parity task IDs, and unverified positives; they should cover off-top-K candidates and multi-token delimiters. The smoke must show verified targets, two applied updates, finite gradients, a saved/exported updated policy, and a fresh rollout from that policy. Held-out panels should report protocol validity, accepted and executed calls, premature closure, repetition, and task solve rate on Pi before/after training, followed by separate cross-harness panels. The control and SFT arm are needed because token-local supervision changes shared model weights; neither global locality nor one-token compute cost is implied. Publish exact pins, cleared examples, verification receipts, costs, and regressions, including a negative result if closure improves without task solves.

## Open questions for the smoke

- Does the pinned Pi parser expose a uniquely accepted closing sequence for each complete payload, including delimiters split across tokens? If several sequences pass, record all and choose a deterministic one before training.
- Does the selected MarinSkyRL runtime expose the same model-visible prefix at candidate scoring and rollout time? Any mismatch should block target admission rather than be silently retokenized.

topics.title: [grug] Add a Pallas-Triton flash attention for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `gpu_pallas_triton_flash`, an opt-in fused causal attention for Grug on AMD GPUs, where Grug has no fused kernel. Existing backends are unchanged.

These kernels use Pallas-Triton, which JAX 0.11 deprecates; Mosaic GPU, the replacement JAX suggests for Pallas, does not support ROCm. #9853 ports the same kernels to Triton launched through `jax_triton.triton_call`, 12-24% faster per layer on MI300X and MI350X, but jax-triton kernels hang multi-GPU training on ROCm today. On a kernel's first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so when the 8 GPUs of one process launch together, all but one fail and the step stalls at the next collective (evidence and a standalone repro in #9853). This PR lands the Pallas-Triton version so AMD runs can use fused attention now. #9853 replaces it once AMD's jax fork, which builds the ROCm plugin, fixes the race.

The kernel reduces each mask to one inclusive key lower bound per query, `max(segment start, q - W + 1)` for window `W`. Key blocks outside `[lower bound, q]` are skipped, and blocks fully inside it skip the mask computation. GQA indexes the shared KV head instead of repeating K/V. Under a mesh, batch and heads may be sharded; sequence and head_dim may not. The lower bounds are computed here and not with the FA4/CuTe helpers, which treat negative segment IDs as padding and would make the ROCm path import the CuTe backend.

One layer's forward plus backward at the June per-GPU shape (8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16), median of three interleaved rounds in one process, jax 0.11.1 (jobs 457836, 457837):

| Mask | GPU | reference | `gpu_pallas_triton_flash` |
|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | MI350X | 20.19 ms | 6.77 ms |
| causal | MI350X | 22.26 ms | 10.04 ms |
| window 2048 | MI300X | 31.17 ms | 12.04 ms |
| causal | MI300X | 32.32 ms | 17.28 ms |

The full June model at batch 64 on 8x MI350X goes from 2.426 s to 1.853 s per step (9.32% to 12.20% MFU) with jaxlib 0.11.0, peak memory falls from 184 to 158 GiB, and the loss matches the reference run (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027803714).

Value and gradient parity tests against `reference_attention` pass on MI350X (job 458164) and in the Pallas interpreter on CPU (job 458155), which is the only way CI runs them. On MI300X the bf16 cases pass and the f32 cases skip (job 458163): Triton runs the kernels' default-precision f32 dots in TF32 on gfx942 and NVIDIA GPUs, about 2.7e-3 off the f32 reference.

Each run of equal segment IDs is one document, so a segment ID that reappears after a different ID starts a new document; `reference_attention` lets the two runs attend to each other. Masks that carry FA4 precomputed bounds are rejected, which excludes the moe_hero_ep, moe_hero_fsdp and fast_track variants.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [levanter] Replace the Pallas short convolution with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
Short convolutions on GPU run in a new streaming Triton kernel that reads each tensor once, instead of once per tap. The Pallas kernel is deleted, and the package moves from `levanter.kernels.pallas.short_conv` to `levanter.kernels.triton.short_conv`. In a single-GPU hero block, short-convolution time per step falls from 4.45 to 1.76 ms.

| Shape | Direction | Previous Pallas | Triton |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | forward | 423.9 us | 226.4 us |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | backward | 1024.3 us | 380.7 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | forward | 103.2 us | 59.3 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | backward | 262.9 us | 105.3 us |

Median kernel time per call on one GB200, 9 documents per sequence. The forward runs at the HBM floor of a read-one-write-one stream on the same tensor, and the backward at 1.14 times its floor. A port of the same algorithm to Pallas reached 230.0 and 403.7 us at C=6144, and needed code-generation workarounds (an inline-asm FMA, program ids clamped to the grid) that steer XLA's Triton pipeline.

The kernel takes kernel size 4, a channel count that is a multiple of 64, and bfloat16 or float32. The wrapper right-pads each local sequence to a multiple of 128 rows with the out-of-range segment id and drops the padded outputs, so any sequence length runs on the kernel. Other calls fall back to `short_conv_reference` with a warning. Every caller gets the kernel, so `GrugModelConfig.sconv_implementation` is removed; checkpoints are unchanged.

The forward and dx are bit-identical to `short_conv_reference` in bfloat16 and float32; dw changes only in fp32 summation order. On SM90 and newer the bf16 multiplies and adds are packed PTX (`mul.rn.bf16x2`, `add.rn.bf16x2`). Older GPUs take an fp32 op and a bf16 cast, which rounds the same way, and Triton's fp fusion is off so that LLVM cannot contract that fallback into a bf16 FMA that rounds once. The fallback has run on GB200 with the capability check forced, but not on an SM80 GPU.

Each program walks a sequence chunk of one channel block. It carries the previous three rows of x (in the backward also the next three rows of dy) and their segment ids in registers, and loads every row of a step before storing any; the backward writes one fp32 dw partial per chunk. A step whose rows lie in one document skips the segment masks, which cuts a backward step from 467 to 275 SASS instructions.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that was 7-15% slower per call shortened the step by 0.55%.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [levanter] Fix reverse slices of sharded flat fields
topics.body: Negative-step slices of sharded cache flat fields returned empty arrays because the reader requested a zero-length forward span. Read the covered span in forward order, then apply the negative stride. Reverse slices now return values across shard boundaries.

topics.title: [grug] Keep hero eval and FLOPs metrics continuous across a relaunch
topics.body:
GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len fixes the held-out eval context independently of the training context, so a run that changes context can keep scoring at 4K and its eval_dropless/* series stays comparable. The dropless eval reports evaluation start and end progress events, as the other evals do.

Per-example FLOPs rise with context length, so the cumulative throughput/total_gflops would jump at a context switch. A FlopsBaseline (completed steps and cumulative FLOPs at the handoff) adds the parent's history to the new shape's count; current MFU uses the new attention cost.

Stacked on #9888. Part of #9615

topics.title: Share Hero and Snowball checkpoint export mechanics
topics.body:
Share bounded HF shard-writing code between Hero and the Levanter converter used by Snowball. Hero reuses the converter's 5 GB file planner; a source tensor larger than that target remains whole. Local files are written directly, while remote files stage under `TMPDIR` before upload.

All JAX ranks replicate tensors in matching order. Only process zero copies weights to CPU and writes files. One writer process supports host-local paths and existing HF upload callbacks. An `ExitStack` owns each memory reservation during gathering; successful submission transfers cleanup to the shard-write task's completion callback. Process zero broadcasts writer failures at matching checks on all ranks.

Hero resume verifies the export request identity and shard checksums before reuse. It writes `export-manifest.json` after all shards and HF metadata to mark completion.

CPU export checks cover exact Hero/Snowball weights, concurrent uploads and two-rank failure/recovery. Full-size accelerator exports and live cloud/HF uploads remain untested.

topics.title: Mine and validate same-history local DPO pairs with datakit
topics.body:
Design, implement, execute, and validate reusable datakit tooling that turns retained agent traces into same-history, single-turn preference examples, then determine whether DPO learns the intended local behavior without degrading task performance. The BFCL campaign already retains traces, preference provenance, task identities, and token masks; verified local-pair extraction remains to be built. [Infrastructure inventory](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/technical-progress-20261011.md).

A bounded bad action is one erroneous tool action or a precisely identified invalid token transition, excluding an arbitrarily long rejected continuation. A verified repair is a replacement supported by explicit protocol, execution, or task-level checks. The preferred and rejected action must share exactly the same conditioning history and tool schema; counterfactual execution also requires equivalent environment state. A later successful retry is not automatically a valid pair because its history contains additional observations.

Datakit is [Marin's data preparation and chat-rendering library](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit); DPO means direct preference optimization. Linked historical reports contain internal provenance paths and withheld-input references; they support public aggregate inspection, not complete independent replay.

Successful calls from otherwise unsuccessful trials are eligible positive examples. Record their evidence level: parser/schema validity, execution success, or task-verifier success. Do not equate these levels or put future tool results into the model's conditioning history.

Done when:

- Audit the existing training-complement corpus and publish eligible counts by harness, task, failure class, and evidence level. Report losses from missing exact histories or unreplayable state; do not presume a large usable yield.
- Implement deterministic extraction for unambiguous repairs and controlled corruptions of verified valid actions. Treat retry mining as a candidate source requiring prefix/state checks. Preserve originals, task/trajectory IDs, hashes, policy/harness versions, repair rules, and verification receipts.
- Emit standard preference artifacts with exact token histories and explicit supervised spans. Bound negative-action length, cap contributions per trajectory/task, deduplicate, and exclude holdout tasks and previously trained task identities as required by the experiment. Validate masks through the production renderer.
- Add behavior-focused tests for identical-prefix enforcement, task leakage, synthetic corruption validity, token-boundary preservation, and mask placement. Distinguish observed negatives from synthetic ones.
- Execute small controlled native DPO runs comparing the extracted local pairs with filtered whole-trace pairs and positive-only masked SFT. Explicitly configure beta, learning rate, sequence/token normalization, masks, batch composition, and reference initialization; vary one factor at a time where possible.
- Demonstrate actual updates and evaluate targeted validity/execution, task success, and cross-harness effects. Publish negative results and a reusable recipe even if DPO does not outperform the simpler control.
- Keep source datasets private unless independently cleared for redistribution; release tooling and aggregate evidence without proprietary harness scaffolding.

[Public collapse analysis](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-collapse-investigation-20261011.md) documents the rejected-loop imbalance motivating bounded examples. It does not prove that this change will repair the model. [Campaign closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040); related work: [localized online feedback #10043](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043) and [online multi-harness integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041).

# Research

The pinned BFCL pipeline retains per-step prompt tokens, response tokens, and loss masks, but its existing preference artifact contains whole trajectories. Pair selection checks the initial prompt and verifier outcome; it does not establish identical conditioning history or environment state at a later tool action. The stopped run's 1,712 pairs came from 633 tasks, and rejected branches had 7.24 times as many supervised tokens as chosen branches ([campaign analysis](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-collapse-investigation-20261011.md)); the public archive cannot establish a usable local-pair count because raw traces are withheld.

- [`data.py#L19-L69`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/data.py#L19-L69) — pinned task identities and holdout

# Proposed design

## Goal and constraint

Produce auditable single-action preference rows and test whether they improve tool behavior without reducing BFCL task success. The first deliverable is a yield audit, since the released aggregates do not show how many private traces have both an exact action prefix and replayable state. Keep source traces and task payloads private; publish tooling, counts, rejection reasons, and screened receipts.

## Plan

1. **Audit the frozen training complement.** Pin collection manifests, task digests, policy and harness revisions, renderer/tokenizer, and initializer training lineage. Stream retained records and native trace/verification receipts without copying bulk source data. Count candidate actions by harness, task, failure class, and evidence level (parser/schema, execution, task verifier); count exclusions for missing exact history, unknown pre-action state, absent receipt, overlength action, duplicate, holdout, and previously trained task ID. A successful call within a failed trial can supply a positive action when its own receipt supports that level of claim. Publish the census before selecting a training recipe.

2. **Add a deterministic datakit extractor and a versioned artifact contract.** Each row carries one exact prompt-token prefix, tool-schema hash, chosen/rejected action token IDs and supervised spans, task/trajectory IDs, source hashes and URIs, policy/harness versions, pre-action state evidence, repair rule/version, verification receipts, evidence level, and whether the negative was observed or synthetic. Form an observed pair only when the token prefix, tool schema, and pre-action state match; a later retry is only a candidate. Generate synthetic negatives by one seeded, bounded corruption of a verified valid action, then check the intended failure with the relevant parser, executor, or task verifier. Reject ambiguous repairs and unverifiable state-dependent comparisons.

3. **Filter and validate before training.** Exclude parity and initializer-trained task identities, deduplicate by task plus prefix and action hashes, and deterministically cap contributions per task and trajectory. Start with a 512-token action limit, four pairs per task, and one pair per trajectory; report the yield under these caps and at 256/1024 tokens before freezing them. Emit the native `chosen_input_ids`/`rejected_input_ids` and assistant-mask columns with identical prefix IDs and zero supervision outside the two action spans. Check token boundaries and masks against the production chat renderer; reject any row whose rendered history differs from the retained prefix. Test prefix/state mismatch, leakage, observed versus synthetic provenance, corruption verdicts, token boundaries, and mask placement using real fixtures.

4. **Run a bounded comparison only if the audit yields enough verified rows.** Freeze one task-disjoint local-pair artifact and matched controls: filtered whole-trajectory DPO and positive-only masked SFT. Use the same initializer, task exposure, evaluation runtime, and policy sampling. Record beta, learning rate, reference initialization, sequence/token normalization, masks, and pair composition explicitly; use the prior beta 0.1 and LR 4e-6 as a documented starting configuration, then change one factor at a time. Verify applied optimizer updates, evaluate action validity/execution and Pi task success at initialization and every four updates, then run complete cross-harness panels for promising checkpoints. Stop a pilot when task success or recognized tool execution collapses, and publish negative results as well as a reusable extraction and training recipe.

## Risks and open questions

Exact token history may be present while equivalent pre-action environment state is not; that reduces observed-pair yield and may leave only synthetic or parser-level examples. The audit should resolve whether retained state fingerprints or replay receipts can support execution-level pairing and whether the proposed contribution caps leave enough task-diverse examples for a meaningful pilot. Do not promote parser-valid actions to task-success labels or infer a win from a small validity improvement without task and cross-harness results.

topics.title: [levanter] Exclude cache markers from Hugging Face mirrors
topics.body:
Skip a Hugging Face repository file when its name matches the configured cache completion marker. The DARE-TIES-02 repository contains `.cache_metadata.json` from its Base cache. During streaming, that file reached the regional mirror before all weight shards. A follower then logged a cache hit on a 90 GB mirror containing only 28 of 39 shards.

The regression test interrupts a weight download and verifies that the marker remains absent until a successful retry. Existing partial mirrors with a copied marker need separate cleanup.

topics.title: [levanter] Stop background iterators after completion
topics.body:
Buffered background iterators now remain stopped after the producer finishes or raises. Previously, consuming the single end marker or error left later `next()` calls waiting forever on an empty queue. Levanter uses this iterator to prefetch data loader batches and evaluation requests.

Regression tests reproduce the hang after normal exhaustion and producer failure in bounded and unbounded queues. The affected safe suite passed 1,063 tests with 13 skips.

topics.title: [grug] Add the H100 pipeline foundation
topics.body:
Add a stage-local JAXPP pipeline for the full MoE model blocks, including latent/shared experts, SConv, attention positions and QB routing. Standard 1F1B remains the default. The synthetic runner supports the main recipe with FP32 parameters, BF16 compute and compute-scaled MuonH; the historical BF16 capacity recipe remains available.

Each routed expert parameter bank now shares one Frobenius norm across its experts, matching the stacked EP model. `--expert-normalization per_expert` provides an explicit comparison mode. `--qb-bias-mode frozen` retains the current pending QB bias while expert and router weights continue updating; adaptive QB remains the default. Numerical CPU regressions cover stacked-versus-stage-local updates and both QB state transitions.

The historical 48-layer, 65K synthetic diagnostic ran on 192 H100s with BF16-stored parameters and per-expert normalization. Its PP24/EP8/CP1 layout placed two layers in each stage and kept expert traffic within eight-GPU workers. It was chosen to establish capacity; no matched PP8/EP32/CP4 Megatron comparison was performed. The README records the later CP2 result and the differences in batch size and attention helpers. Historical hardware results do not validate the new normalization or frozen-QB option, and no SFT/RL quality comparison has been run.

The affected safe suite passed 2,391 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Focused CPU checks passed 86 tests with one skip; required lint, full type checking, strict docs and source links passed.

#9662 is stacked above this foundation and adds checkpoint/data support, the GB200 launcher, tracked runtime setup and bounded main-recipe hardware validation. Before merge, this foundation still owns replacing the positional result from `initialize_stage_local_pipeline_state`, centralizing the repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers, and separating the synthetic runner lifecycle in `pipeline_smoke.main`. These deferred changes require compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation; #9662 then owns adapting its added checkpoint/data lifecycle.

topics.title: [grug] Add a Triton flash attention for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `gpu_triton_flash`, an opt-in fused causal attention for Grug on AMD GPUs, where Grug had no fused kernel. Existing backends are unchanged. The forward, dQ and dK/dV kernels are Triton kernels launched through `jax_triton`, like the top-k and Sonic MoE kernels. Earlier revisions of this PR used the Pallas Triton backend. JAX 0.11 deprecates it and tells Triton users to switch to the official Triton bindings and `jax_triton`; its other route, Pallas on Mosaic GPU, does not target AMD GPUs.

The kernels reduce each mask to one inclusive key lower bound per query, `max(segment start, q - W + 1)` for window `W`. Key blocks outside `[lower bound, q]` are skipped, and blocks fully inside it skip the mask computation. GQA indexes the shared KV head instead of repeating K/V. The dK/dV kernel computes `K Qᵀ`, so P and dS come out of their matmuls already transposed for the dV and dK matmuls. Under a mesh, batch and heads may be sharded; sequence and head_dim may not.

One layer's forward plus backward at the June model's per-GPU shape (8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16), median of three interleaved rounds in one process (jobs 457836, 457837):

| Mask | GPU | reference | Pallas Triton (earlier revision) | `gpu_triton_flash` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | MI350X | 20.19 ms | 6.77 ms | 5.11 ms |
| causal | MI350X | 22.26 ms | 10.04 ms | 8.38 ms |
| window 2048 | MI300X | 31.17 ms | 12.04 ms | 10.17 ms |
| causal | MI300X | 32.32 ms | 17.28 ms | 15.25 ms |

Pallas hands its Triton IR to XLA's bundled Triton, while `jax_triton` compiles with pip triton 3.6. With the Pallas revision's tiles, the port ran 11-13% slower than Pallas, so the tiles were swept again on both GPUs. MI350X (gfx950) runs the forward with two pipeline stages and MI300X with one; the other tiles are shared.

Value and gradient parity tests against `reference_attention` pass on MI300X and MI350X. CI has neither a GPU nor jax-triton, so it skips them. All dots run at IEEE precision: by default Triton runs float32 dots as xf32 on MI300X, which failed the float32 tests. Float32 inputs get smaller tiles, because the bf16 tiles overflow MI300X's 64 KiB of shared memory.

On ROCm the kernels need jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer with jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6; jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher. The measurements above used jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0. #9989 moves the HPC Fund venv recipe to these versions.

Each run of equal segment IDs is one document, so a segment ID that reappears after a different ID starts a new document; `reference_attention` lets the two runs attend to each other. Masks that carry FA4 precomputed bounds are rejected, which excludes the moe_hero_ep, moe_hero_fsdp and fast_track variants.

jax-triton kernels fail today when one process drives several AMD GPUs: on a kernel's first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so all but one GPU fail and the step stalls at the next collective (repro in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9853#issuecomment-6090140907). #10014 lands the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels in the meantime; this PR replaces it once AMD's jax fork fixes the race.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [analysis] Independent pre-registered forecast of the hero's final loss, with 80/95% intervals
topics.body: Hi @ClassicLarry @dlwh, To add uncertainty to the Aug 19 pre-registration in #8435, I made an independent forecast of the hero's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` (4K eval packing). It is frozen at 58% of training and uses only public data. **Result:** median **2.035**, 80% interval [2.023, 2.047], 95% [2.016, 2.054]. The Aug 19 pre-registration (2.039) sits at our 68th percentile, so the run looks on track for it. A finish near 2.10 looks very unlikely. **Method in brief** - The ladder is used only for the remaining drop from now to the end. The level comes from the hero's own post-swap evals, which makes the forecast nearly independent of the floor E. - Backtests set the drift persistence, the method error and an allowance for distance-dependent bias. They use held-out ladder rungs and the 67B-A2B run (#6044). In nested leave-one-out, the 80% intervals cover 14–15 of 16 held-out cases. - PTB gets its own term because of its noise and the exposures in #9874. A PTB-free companion target is forecast too: 2.047 [2.036, 2.059]. **One finding:** most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap comes from counting lm_head FLOPs in compute. On the H100 d768–d1536 runs, excluding them moves the fitted floor from 1.913 to 1.573 and the forecast from 2.116 to 2.037 (see the comment below for the refit's exact setting). **Pre-registration, code and scoring rules:** https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/prereg-v2-2026-10-09/preregistration_v2.md - The scoring rules were fixed in advance, including what happens if the context or the schedule changes. - This is v2. I revised v1 (median 2.045) the same day after re-auditing its backtests, on the same data. Both versions are tagged, and every change is listed. - I'll post a check-in at 70% and the scored comparison after the run ends.

topics.title: [grug] Leave ragged MoE transport rows unwritten when nothing reads them
topics.body:
The ragged all-to-all MoE stops zero-filling and overwriting transport rows that no consumer reads, and on GPU builds its dispatch buffer with one scatter. Outputs, drops and gradients are bitwise unchanged. One MoE layer's forward and backward is 4.4-4.8% faster and its compiler temp 1.37 GB smaller, and the hero step shortens by 1.41% (13.732 to 13.541 s against #9831, over 26 scored steps).

The expert chunks write disjoint rows of the dispatch and return buffers, but the custom VJP around `ragged_all_to_all` differentiated each write as an overwrite, so every layer's backward spent a [TK, H] select, add and zero fill on rows the next chunk would ignore. Each written row holds nothing before its one write, and for such a row an overwrite has the derivative of an add, so the transpose passes the output cotangent through unchanged. With every consumer reading only rows a collective wrote, the buffers need no fill: on GPU they come from a Triton kernel that writes nothing, elsewhere they are zero-filled. Each buffer is tied to a loop-carried value, because XLA would otherwise hoist an input-free buffer out of the layer loop and copy it into every layer's output slot. Dropped and padded slots get combine weight 0, and the combine and dispatch-gradient sums skip them. A GPU test fills every buffer with NaN instead of zero and requires identical outputs, drop counts and gradients under 22 routings, among them an expert no token selects, a receiver chunk and a whole receiver with no rows, a sender with only padding, and near-total drops, with two chunks of three experts per GPU as on the hero.

On GPU, a Triton kernel builds the expert-sorted dispatch buffer by reading each token's row once and writing it to the token's accepted slots, where a gather read every row topk times: 0.535 ms (6.6 TB/s) at the hero's per-GPU routed shape (TK = 524288 rows of the 3072-wide latent). Its weighted form serves #9833's backward. The gather-sum's forward loops over 1024-wide hidden tiles, which keeps more programs resident: 0.508 ms against 0.574 ms.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0), each head compiled fresh.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [iris] Take periodic k8s thread dumps without pausing the process
topics.body:
`PeriodicProfiler` dumps every running Kubernetes task pod's threads every 10 minutes. It used py-spy's default `dump`, which stops the target process while it reads the stacks. In a job whose processes synchronize frequently, a pause on any process stalls the others. On a 704-GPU training run, each sweep cost 7–10 s of step time, about 1.3% of throughput.

Periodic dumps now pass `--nonblocking`, so py-spy reads the stacks from the running process. On one GB200 rack (64 training processes), sweeps that dumped one pod at a time cost 0.67–0.93 s of step time with blocking dumps and 0–0.05 s with `--nonblocking`. Scaled to 704 processes, the blocking cost predicts about 9 s per sweep. One of 48 non-blocking pod dumps failed with `Bad address (os error 14)`; the profiler skips a failed capture for that cycle, as it already does for any failed dump. On-demand dumps keep pausing for a consistent read. `build_pyspy_dump_cmd` rejects `--nonblocking` combined with `--native`, which py-spy 0.4.2 refuses.

The change takes effect when the CoreWeave controller restarts; running pods need no restart.

topics.title: [post-training] Compare SFT, rejection-sampled SFT and OPD transfer on Snowball with CruxEval
topics.body:
Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LVfMDHRBKBk_Bn9PY1J9Lb_MYwdUTFP5PkX2br25TNg/edit?tab=t.izhzsywzorld. Final results and the full ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 (ledger also at https://gist.github.com/karansag/0ce1a07580bd430bc8c5b890069385b0).

**TL;DR (final, 2026-10-09).** Given one expert E built from the Snowball student B by SFT on GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces, three methods were used to transfer E's gain back into B: plain SFT on E's traces, SFT on rejection-sampled E traces (RS-SFT), and on-policy distillation from E (OPD). All three recover most or all of E's CruxEval gain on the 1,600 training-is-test prompts. Two-pass CruxEval input / output accuracy on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0, RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9, OPD 79.6 / 75.2, against E 79.4 / 71.4 and B 55.4 / 57.8. RS-SFT and OPD are both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering (1.2 / 2.7 pp) is unresolved with one run per arm and two evaluator passes. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K or MATH500. Training cost: plain SFT 61.6 H100-h, RS-SFT 57.4, OPD 376.4 for the full run (286.9 to the selected checkpoint, plus 14–15 per HF export). RS-SFT used ground-truth execution results to select demos; the other arms did not. These numbers measure transfer on seen prompts, not generalization.

**Results (selected checkpoints; CruxEval two-pass means, pass@1 %, 800 problems per direction; "gap closed" = gain over B divided by E's gain over B).**

| Model | CruxEval input | CruxEval output | Gap closed (in / out) | GSM8K | MATH500 | Training H100-h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B (student) | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 | — |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — | — |
| E (expert; B + SFT on GLM traces, step 272) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 | 35.9 |
| Plain SFT on E demos, 400 updates (final) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 | 61.6 |
| RS-SFT on execution-correct E demos, 283 of 376 updates | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 | 57.4 (full run) |
| OPD from E, 75 of 100 updates | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 | 286.9 to the checkpoint; 376.4 full run; +14–15 per HF export |

**Models.** Student B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`. E = B after full SFT on 1,454 execution-correct GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 272 updates, 32 H100, fresh optimizer state, frozen router biases), export `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`. E keeps B's tokenizer and chat template. E+ (E + 2 epochs at LR 1e-6; 80.2 / 75.1) was built as a separate reference and is not an arm. Every arm starts from B.

**Benchmark.** CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped as the target because B already scores 89.8% there; GSM8K and MATH500 are the collapse checks. Teacher gate: B 55.4 / 57.8; GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts 94.0 / 90.5; E 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean), passing the gate of B + 10 points on both tasks with no GSM8K drop.

**Frozen evaluator.** Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy `c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2`, vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). One pass on 800 problems has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp; selected checkpoints get two passes.

**Arms as run (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the 1,600 prompts; one checkpoint per epoch).**
- E demos: 8 samples per prompt from E at temperature 1.0, both directions, execution-graded in an isolated container (12,800 samples, 14.6 H100-h, shared by both SFT arms).
- Plain SFT: E's first sample per prompt, correct or not (1,600 rows; 1.45M supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16; Levanter, 32 H100).
- RS-SFT: first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows; 97 prompts with no correct sample stay in the eval denominator; 1.06M supervised tokens per epoch; Levanter, 32 H100).
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, 4 on-policy rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E as the teacher (sampled reverse KL on chosen tokens, no verifier), 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch; 4 learner + 1 rollout + 1 teacher H100x8 nodes (Megatron).
- Selection: the final checkpoint when it is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions, otherwise a second pass on both and the two-pass means decide. Plain SFT selected its final checkpoint (400 updates); RS-SFT (283 of 376) and OPD (75 of 100) selected their epoch-3 checkpoints after their finals dropped on one direction.

**Artifacts.** Trace browser (GLM, E, E+ traces, side-by-side compare): https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/. OPD W&B: marin-community/skyrl run p3ie2bg7. Selected exports: plain `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`, RS-SFT `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`, OPD `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`. Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/<record>/record.json`.

**Not in scope.** Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval).

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher.
- 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro (B 44.1) and GPQA-D (B 41.9) measured as fallbacks and not used.
- 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain.
- 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm.
- 2026-10-08: E frozen at step 272 for every arm; E+ built as a separate reference only. Arms changed from the plan: one sample per prompt for both SFT arms (not up to 4), no LR sweep, 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD. The arms ran in parallel on Iris.
- 2026-10-09: RS-SFT and OPD final checkpoints not selected (drops on one direction with paired CI excluding 0); epoch-3 checkpoints selected on two-pass means. Final results posted in one comment; the running-log comments were removed and are archived with the ledger.

topics.title: [grug] Separate model and data fast tracks
topics.body:
* keep the model track on `hero_tok/v16384_shuf/train` and add two independent Zephyr data tracks
* for a new dataset, sample the Hero production mixture from `harrier_mix_2026_08_18.json` and its pinned `datakit/store_4d2e363d` source store
  * preserve seeded component loader order and retokenize with `hero-bpe-v16384`
  * set fraction `p` of the final training mix to new data
  * scale the existing Hero weights by `1 - p`.
  * require the available token count. Reuse one bounded Hugging Face prefix across scales and simulate the production epoch count.
  * do not apply topic or quality classifiers to this track.
* for quality experiments, sample raw text from all 292 registered DataKit sources in proportion to available corpus size, without topic clusters or Hero mixture weights
  * reject missing source pins. Use a seeded cyclic interval in the document-ID hash space and omit only row groups with proven-disjoint ID statistics.
  * this is a hash-interval sample; document inclusion events are not independent Bernoulli draws.
  * each ladder rung specifies a model size and training-token budget. Prepare 174,787,133,440 raw tokens for the largest 17,478,713,344-token MoE rung.
  * prepare features and scores for the 174,787,133,440-token raw pool once. Reuse those scores across smaller rungs.
  * for separately prepared features, require independent expected normalized-text and Harrier-output paths for every raw source, with exact agreement between the pins and the prepared artifact.
  * at each rung, take a prefix from the fixed, seeded random document order, with ten times that rung's training budget. Reject constant candidate or incumbent scores within that prefix and preserve the original document locators.
  * rank documents by classifier score. Select documents from the highest scores until their token total fills the training budget.
  * fit a ridge head to frozen GLM quality targets and cached Harrier features.
  * exclude every document ID from the original GLM label export, including IDs without joined features. Also exclude duplicate groups from joined label text.
  * for repeated document IDs with identical text and targets, keep the first embedding in sorted path/row order. Record vector differences in a content-hashed report.
  * choose `features`, `score`, `select`, or `train` with `--stage`. Use `--scored-pool` for reuse and `--moe` for MoE models. Reject options that the selected stage cannot use.
* keep the DataKit workflow available through `uv run fast-track --source-mode sample`.
* the earlier dense Hero-mix pilot completed three matched d512 baseline/treatment seed pairs at 361,758,720 tokens per run.
  * BPB means bits per byte. Higher BPB is worse
  * a rebuild under the long-string policy preserved all 52,746 WikiText rows and 4,194,501 tokens in exact order.
  * a 10% WikiText mixture did not improve the Paloma or Uncheatable macro score in these three pairs. No larger rung started.
  * at seed 0, a 99% mixture increased Paloma BPB from 1.5290 to 2.8578 and Uncheatable BPB from 1.2353 to 2.5097.
  * these disposable probes use assumed production counts of 10B total tokens and 100M available new-dataset tokens. They do not establish production dataset value.
* the real GLM/Harrier probe froze 79,335 labeled documents and fit a ridge head with development MSE 0.03946
  * a separate calculation reproduced all scores in the 307-document integration pool
* the earlier four-source quality pilot prepared 6,064,023 documents and 3,617,587,227 tokens from `cp/arxiv_abstracts`, `cp/wikiteam`, `docx-corpus/en`, and `starcoder2/documentation`
  * ridge scores ranged from 0.0244 to 1.0080, with low-score withdrawal notices and damaged pages as well as technical text in the private document sample
  * matched dense d512 seed-0 runs each used 361,758,720 tokens, the same model configuration, and unchanged evaluation sets
  * quality-selected versus random-selection Paloma macro BPB: 1.9051 versus 1.6164. Uncheatable: 1.5914 versus 1.3522
  * 20 of 23 dataset metrics were worse after quality selection. No larger rung started
  * one-seed, four-source pilot only. Selection also changes source and length distributions. Evaluation text overlap remains unaudited
  * [quality-selected run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fft9371-quality-ridge4-candidate-d512-s0-20261004) and [random control](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fft9371-quality-ridge4-random-d512-s0-20261004) both succeeded

* use `fast-track-long-string-v1` for Hugging Face and raw-corpus tokenization
  * use the production tokenizer's 10,000-character split mechanism to bound long-string encoding
  * preserve full text and document identity. Token IDs can change at split boundaries.
  * bound text batches and reject a sampled document above 64 MiB with document context. Do not drop or truncate it.
  * bound native tokenizer batches without changing the existing text split points. Keep native batch behavior for padding and stochastic BPE configurations.
  * a local 32 MiB sampler probe preserved all 19,532,169 token IDs. Bounded native batches reduced peak RSS from 4.60 GiB to 2.85 GiB.
  * synthetic short-document batches took 4–8% more time in three-repeat median comparisons. These measurements do not establish production throughput.
  * the first four-source preparation exceeded an 8 GiB worker limit. Its replacement stopped on two 38 MB documents above the previous 32 MiB document limit.
  * the two real documents passed exact-token comparisons at 2.31 and 2.40 GiB peak RSS. Four synthetic 64 MiB cases stayed below 4.86 GiB peak RSS.
  * a document one byte above 64 MiB failed with source and document context. The corrected preparation and matched training pilot succeeded
* bound pending token-cache buffers by bytes and document count while preserving token order and cache metadata
  * one `cw-us-east-02a` 6,350-document prefix benchmark reduced median cache-write time from 6.24 seconds to 0.773 seconds, with identical ordered token hashes
  * this measures one 4,194,548-token prefix, not full-pipeline throughput. The largest measured RSS was about 899 MiB
* the final focused suite passed all 92 fast-track and disposable Focus-feature tests; required lint and type checks passed
  * the full affected suite had 6,043 passes and 18 failures. One changed CLI test read the wrong nested trainer field; it passed after that assertion was corrected.
  * fresh serial checks found ten current passes, including the corrected CLI test. Five storage failures matched the clean baseline and passed on both checkouts with local scratch storage.
  * one C++ reward mismatch and two 60-second JAX timeouts also occurred on clean baseline `6940dbb764856c9b286eac3b800e3fa36b0753a0`. No branch-only failure was found. The timeouts remain unresolved.
  * no numerical tolerance, marker, or per-test timeout changed
* four-scale MoE validation is in progress at d512, d768, d1024, and d1280
  * reuse one completed maximum Hero sample and one completed WikiText prefix. The disposable exposure probes declare 20B production tokens and 100M available new-dataset tokens.
  * the d512 Hero baseline, 10% WikiText mix, and 99% WikiText mix each completed at 1,250,426,880 tokens. At seed 0, both mixtures worsened all 23 dataset BPB scores.
  * versus Hero, the 10% mix increased Paloma macro BPB by 4.07% and Uncheatable macro BPB by 1.97%; the 99% mix increased them by 58.98% and 72.54%.
  * the d768 Hero baseline completed at 3,633,315,840 tokens. The remaining matched comparisons are not complete.
  * one d768 99% launch stopped during W&B setup because its command omitted offline mode. The failed run is retained; it is not a dataset-quality result.
  * a [CPU-node incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/607) caused Iris to retry both d1024 parents and restart their GPU children from zero. Checkpoint saving was disabled; no manual restart was made.
  * the all-292-source raw quality pool is still in preparation. Its quality-training comparisons have not started.
  * these single-seed checks do not establish a production-data improvement. Experiment scripts remain outside the branch.

The following DataKit design and experiment record precedes the separate Hero-mix and quality tracks. The DataKit sample target is 25B input tokens across all 292 registered sources, with corpus-size sampling weights recorded in its completion manifest. Training rejects a store with fewer usable tokens than the requested budget. The ladder includes model widths of 512, 768, 1024, and 1280, each with dense and MoE variants. The largest default ladder run requires 17,478,713,344 usable tokens.

Run source-recipe, embedding, quality, assignment, and centroid-sampling drivers in the pipeline coordinator with up to 64 concurrent steps. The 292-source registry graph has one remote artifact-step job instead of 879. Moving those source drivers from remote jobs to the coordinator preserves all 2,477 artifact identities.

Centroid training remains remote. Within each DataKit fast-track run, all Zephyr stages share one worker with 120 CPUs, 1900 GiB RAM, and 25 TiB disk, without GPU reservation. This profile reserves about 94% each of the allocatable CPU, RAM, and disk capacity on an RNO2A H100 node. Registry-mode download and normalization also use this pool. Tasks retain their resource requests, with CPU and RAM admission limits. Model training uses a separate 8-H100 job.

The Zephyr coordinator permits 68 concurrent pipelines and uses 100 RPC threads. Fray passes actor concurrency to Iris through the fix from [PR #8497](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8497). The previous 32-thread limit let pipeline waits block worker heartbeats.

JAX coordinator names include the full child job token and attempt number. This prevents a training job from connecting to another child job’s JAX coordinator. The sibling naming approach comes from [PR #8941](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8941). This change retains the existing attempt isolation.

The data artifact path includes the terminal DataKit store identity and tokenizer vocabulary size. Runs with the same recipe and version reuse that artifact, independent of their training run IDs. Changes to source recipes, tokenizer identity, or cluster configuration select a different artifact path. Set a new `fast-track --version` to rebuild the outer artifact while retaining unchanged upstream caches.

The sample builder writes its completion record after every source succeeds. `--source-mode cache` selects the existing `hero_tok/v16384_shuf/train` cache.

DataKit drivers install CPU dependencies. GPU setup reinstalls the installed CUDA toolchain version when its `ptxas` binary is missing. Artifact loading restores absolute bucket paths. Disabled W&B mode reaches the GPU tasks.

The negative control reads a completed baseline store and shuffles ordinary tokens within each document. Document order, lengths, token counts, and special-token positions stay unchanged.

DataKit groups documents by content cluster and quality range. Each bucket can contain documents from several sources. Training samples each bucket in proportion to its token count. It uses training seed 0 and the same [ladder model and budget defaults](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/rav/e2e-data/experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py) as the baseline. Evaluation data stays unchanged.

The [25B sample job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Ffast-track-sample-25b-20261002) succeeded in 9 minutes 37 seconds. Its verified manifest contains all 292 sources and their sampling weights. The sample occupies 34.6 GiB.

The completed store contains 29,858,746,027 usable tokens across 39 buckets and 18,236,230 documents across all 40 buckets. One bucket has only 974 tokens, below the 4,096-token training sequence length. The usable-token count sums all tokens in buckets with at least one full sequence. It does not round each bucket down to full sequences.

The store source list matches the sample manifest. The store occupies 37.3 GiB and exceeds the largest ladder budget. The 25B sampling target estimates input size, so it differs from the measured token count.

The initial data attempt used four Iris jobs: the pipeline coordinator, Zephyr coordinator, one worker, and centroid training. No per-source driver jobs appeared. topics.title: [iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures
topics.body:
Add bounded S3 write/read/delete probes to the Kubernetes node agent. Each probe uses the task storage endpoint and credentials and writes a small scratch object per node incarnation. The controller cordons persistent outliers only after a fresh majority of nodes successfully probes the same target after the failure began. Node UID, boot ID, report freshness, environment revision, and Kubernetes resource versions fence stale evidence and concurrent changes.

Group checks under `kubernetes_provider.node_health` with a shared cordon budget. The production `cw-rno2a`, `cw-us-east-02a`, and `cw-us-east-08a` configs probe the shared `marin-us-east-02a` bucket under one-day scratch expiry. The node agent continues probing while cordoned. A fresh success from the current node and configured target after the cordon uncordons a node quarantined by Iris and releases its budget, including after a reboot or credential rotation. Operator cordons remain. Running tasks are not evicted.

Health and cordon evidence remain in node annotations when Finelog is unavailable. Configuration, scratch-object lifecycle, and recovery are documented in the CoreWeave guide. The node-local storage failure that motivated this check is recorded in the [hero incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599).

topics.title: [grafana] Prepare GPU history by requested priority
topics.body:
Prepare seven-day H100 and Blackwell (GB200) allocation-history panels grouped by each child job's requested priority. An Interactive request dispatched as Batch stays in the Interactive group. There is no applied-priority lookup or toggle. Iris and Finelog server code, persisted schemas, retention and writes are unchanged.

The projection sums requested GPU sizes over recorded attempt execution intervals at common sampling instants, with cadence chosen from the selected range: one minute through six hours, five minutes through two days, and fifteen minutes through seven days. Exact historical pod binding/cleanup intervals and allocatable capacity remain unavailable. The requested-GPU series therefore recovers only part of allocation; every point is marked incomplete and idle stays blank. Missing regional inputs leave blank spans. Coverage compares Finelog per-root Running task counts with retained attempt intervals, including CPU tasks; differences flag incomplete or inconsistent task history. It also reports setup tasks and unresolved GPU models. Without assignment creation times, the reader cannot establish when setup began, so setup GPU quantities stay blank.

The production metadata reader remains to be implemented and wired; without one the bridge returns HTTP 503. An approved temporary pilot used Grafana's actual CW service identity plus five-minute Iris dashboard-role cookies over the public Kubernetes controller proxy in all three regions. Existing job/resource/full-retry reads succeeded, GetCurrentUser reported dashboard, and SELECT1 was denied by Iris with HTTP 403. All temporary Role/RoleBinding objects were deleted and absence verified; Grafana's original proxy403 returned afterward. No production grants, credentials or deployment remain from the pilot. The minimal tested transport scope is services/proxy on iris/iris-controller-svc:10000; this reader's POST RPCs need the Kubernetes create verb, plus separate read-only Iris authentication.

A straightforward job/task-API reader would require at least 44,398 inventory calls over the captured sampled cohort, before additional pages and full-retry calls. This is a request-count estimate, not measured production latency. Existing controller backups offer a possible bulk alternative without controller changes: recent backups exist in all three regions. One GB200 backup was 25.4 MB compressed and 421.6 MB decompressed; it downloaded in 1.17s, decompressed in 0.22s, and returned 5,712 retained attempts in a 0.032s immutable local SQL query on devbox. Regional coverage, Cloud Run memory/refresh cost, and scoped object-read credentials still need validation before choosing and wiring that reader. Existing backups already contain requested band and current task band; older attempts do not have their own applied-band field.

All 421 Grafana tests and pre-commit checks passed. The requested-only preview uses captured task-state and regional metadata, with 672 common fifteen-minute instants per model. Every point is incomplete; 226 instants show a difference between per-root Running counts and retained intervals. Earlier applied-view replay timings are retained as prior measurements; production requested-reader loading and refresh costs remain unmeasured.

topics.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
topics.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

topics.title: Plateau Dropping: per-token loss-plateau gating for agentic SFT
topics.body: # Plateau Dropping: per-token loss-plateau gating for agentic SFT **Summary.** Track every token's SFT loss across epochs and stop the gradient from tokens whose loss has plateaued; let them re-enter if their loss moves again. On the Grug 09.21 base and the run7 agentic mix this gives +4 pp pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2 and +5 pp on TB-Lite over plain SFT, holds the gain through pass@4, and matches plain SFT at pass@8. A random-drop control equals plain SFT and a confidence-only drop is worse than plain SFT, so the loss history is what matters. Preliminary SWE-bench Verified numbers after SFT on Open-SWE-Traces show a larger gap. ## Method - For each trained token position (document, offset) keep its loss at the last two visits and a visit count. - From a token's third visit on, if its last two visit-to-visit relative loss changes are both < 10 % (with a 0.05-nat floor on the denominator), its loss term is masked out of the batch loss. The token still goes through the forward pass and still sits in the context; only its gradient contribution is removed. If its loss moves again, it re-enters. - Everything else is plain SFT: same data, learning rate, window, batch, and schedule; the loss is averaged over kept tokens. - On the run7 mix about 65 % of tokens are dropped per batch once every token has three visits: ~60 % because they are learned (loss < 0.1 nats), ~5 % because they never move (example-specific paths, hashes). The all-token training loss stays within 0.005 nats of plain SFT. Loosely inspired by GRPO discarding all-correct and all-wrong groups: positions that carry no learning signal stop driving the update. TailSFT (trajectory-level) and turn-level variants of it did not move pass@k over plain SFT on these tasks. ## Setup - Base: Grug 67B-A2B 09.21. Data: run7 mix, 6,301 MiniSweAgent trajectories / 45.0M tokens / 1,610 tasks (5,324 allenai/tmax-sft successes from Qwen3.6-27B + 977 reward-1 rollouts of the base model on Endless Terminals + Recursive-Task-Synthesis). 32k window, lr 1e-4, one pass = 21.5 steps. - Arms: plain SFT 66 steps (3 ep, the run7 checkpoint), plain SFT 220 steps (10 ep, matched compute), plateau dropping 220 and 440 steps (10 and 20 ep), plus the base model. - Eval: all 89 TB2 and 100 TB-Lite tasks, MiniSweAgent harness, 3x task timeouts, temperature 1, one vLLM server per attempt, 8 attempts per task (base: 3). pass = reward 1; timeouts count as failures; trials that died on infrastructure errors are discarded. pass@k is the unbiased estimator; each panel uses every task with >= k valid attempts in all arms shown; error bars are SE over tasks. Every number was recounted independently and matches harbor's own job summaries. ## Results TB2 (88 / 88 / 88 / 74 matched tasks): | arm | pass@1 | pass@2 | pass@4 | pass@8 | |---|---|---|---|---| | base 09.21, no SFT | 8.5 | 13.3 | - | - | | plain SFT, 3 ep (66 steps) | 9.8 | 15.8 | 23.6 | 35.1 | | plain SFT, 10 ep (220 steps) | 11.8 | 17.4 | 23.4 | 31.1 | | plateau dropping, 10 ep (220 steps) | 11.7 | 18.7 | 26.1 | 33.8 | | plateau dropping, 20 ep (440 steps) | **14.1** | **20.4** | **26.7** | 31.1 | TB-Lite (98 / 98 / 98 / 90 matched tasks): | arm | pass@1 | pass@2 | pass@4 | pass@8 | |---|---|---|---|---| | plain SFT, 3 ep | 21.8 | 32.9 | 44.1 | 54.4 | | plain SFT, 10 ep | 21.4 | 32.0 | 43.0 | 55.6 | | plateau dropping, 10 ep | 24.1 | 35.3 | 47.4 | **60.0** | | plateau dropping, 20 ep | **26.6** | **38.8** | **49.6** | 57.8 | Paired against the 3-epoch plain checkpoint, the 20-epoch run is +4.2 +- 2.1 (TB2) and +4.8 +- 1.7 (TB-Lite) at pass@1. The gain narrows as k grows: at pass@8 the 10-epoch run holds it on TB-Lite (+5.6 +- 4.6) and is level on TB2; the 20-epoch run is level on TB-Lite and gives back a few points on TB2 (-4.1 +- 4.1). The rule makes the model solve the same tasks more reliably rather than solve new ones. Plain SFT at 10 epochs sharpens too but loses coverage (TB2 pass@8 -4.1). ## Ablations (220 steps, drop from step 65, 3 attempts, paired vs plain 3 ep) | arm | TB2 pass@1 | TB-Lite pass@1 | |---|---|---| | random 65 % of tokens dropped | +2.9 +- 2.8 (= plain SFT 10 ep) | -0.8 +- 3.2 | | confidence-only drop (p > 0.9, no history) | -1.9 +- 2.1 | **-11.5 +- 3.1** | | plateau dropping, 10 ep | +2.9 +- 2.9 | +4.1 +- 2.9 | | plateau dropping, 20 ep | +7.2 +- 2.7 | +4.5 +- 2.9 | | EMA variant of the plateau test, 20 ep | +7.2 +- 3.6 | -1.2 +- 3.1 | | plateau dropping, 40 ep | +6.3 +- 2.9 | +4.5 +- 3.4 | Random dropping = plain SFT; dropping by confidence alone hurts; 40 epochs adds nothing over 20; the EMA variant keeps the TB2 gain and loses the TB-Lite one. ## SWE-bench Verified (preliminary) Both arms SFT'd for 20 passes (1,520 steps, 64k window) on nvidia/Open-SWE-Traces v1.2 mini-swe-agent trajectories (Qwen3.8-27B thinking teacher, resolved, one bash call per turn, 9,229 trajectories / 319M tokens), evaluated under the same MiniSweAgent harness on a random 100 of SWE-bench Verified, 3 attempts. With ~40 % of trials in: plateau dropping ~38 % pass@1 vs ~17 % for plain SFT and ~17 % for the base; paired on common tasks +21 +- 5. Trajectory checks show both arms are format-healthy (< 2 % turns without a tool call). Final numbers to follow.
