topics.title: [grafana] Bound bridge memory during queries and pod scans
topics.body:
Release query inputs when a cached failure is recorded, and allow at most two dashboard computations, with each slot held from source loading through projection. Cached errors preserve their message and HTTP classification without retaining traceback locals or response bodies. Arrow cache accounting includes full referenced buffers.

Stream Kubernetes pod scans one page at a time and query watched deployments directly for the control-plane crashloop alert. Malformed Kubernetes JSON responses produce HTTP upstream failures rather than partial results. Keep Grafana's Cloud Run memory limit at 4 GiB in Pulumi.

The incident exhausted both the previous 2 GiB limit and a 4 GiB replacement. Local reproductions retained 192 MiB through failed queries in a cache capped at 128 MiB; the change releases those tables. A 2,500-pod synthetic scan fell from 108 MiB to 32 MiB peak Python allocations with identical results. These reproductions establish memory defects; they do not identify every contributor to the production OOMs.

[Incident and reproduction details](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/655).

topics.title: [levanter] Preserve staged mixture indices beyond 2^31
topics.body:
Staged mixtures now preserve child indices when a stage begins after 2^31 samples. Cumulative counts previously used 32-bit storage, and multiplying a stage's block count by samples per block also overflowed before accumulation. Reads in the next stage could therefore use negative child indices.

A regression reads across this boundary through `MixtureDataset.get_batch`. The selected suite reported 1,235 passes, 6 skips, and one parallel worker crash in `test_train_lm_fp8`; that test passed on its isolated rerun.

topics.title: [levanter] Bound in-flight W&B metric host copies
topics.body:
Keep at most 8 device-to-host copies ahead of the value being read when converting a W&B payload. #9600 started a copy for every array leaf at once.

PJRT's GPU client finishes pending copies on a work queue (`pjrt_async_work_runner`) that starts a thread whenever queued work exceeds its idle threads and never stops one. A step's outputs become ready together, so prefetching a watch-step payload released thousands of copies at once and grew the queue by hundreds of threads in every process. The threads inherit the name `py_xla_callback` because their own name exceeds Linux's 15-character limit. On a one-rack restore of the hero run, each training process grew from 1 to about 1,700 `py_xla_callback` threads within 20 minutes, about 3,400 threads in total. Each blocking py-spy dump pauses every thread, so dumps took about 3.5x longer; #9998 makes Iris's periodic dumps non-blocking.

A single-node GB200 repro (4 processes, d768 MoE, watch every 10 steps) puts the growth at #9600: its parent and main with #9600 reverted keep 1 `py_xla_callback` thread per process, and #9600 has 318–424. With 2,000 scalars converted by `_convert_metrics_to_wandb_loggable` on one GPU:

| | `py_xla_callback` threads | conversion time |
|---|---|---|
| before #9600 | 1 | 60 ms |
| #9600 | 418 | 31 ms |
| this change | 2 | 33 ms |

topics.title: [rolloutengine] Grade reasoning-only truncated responses
topics.body:
Reasoning-only model responses with `content=null` no longer interrupt grading preparation. The rollout record retains the raw message, token evidence, and `length` stop reason while grading evidence represents the missing answer as empty assistant content.

Text answer tasks report a submission failure. File tasks can grade files written before truncation, including when the model ends at its generation limit.

Fixes #10031

topics.title: [grug] Hide the hero's bare MoE transports behind shared and chunk GEMMs
topics.body:
Under the hero's carry offload, every MoE transport except one ~1 ms routing-weight return now runs beside a GEMM, which shortens the step by 0.73% (12.730 to 12.638 s) and cuts exposed collective time from 1.19 to 0.85 s/step. Before, with one collective in flight, the first forward dispatch and both recomputed dispatches of the backward ran bare (0.63 s/step), and small collectives inside the routed-MoE section held the slot through expert GEMMs. Three changes that only work together fix the schedule:

- The MLP section's FSDP weight all-gathers, the QB router statistics and the drop count complete before the first dispatch. The statistics are saved for the backward, so its recompute does not rerun their all-reduces.
- The routed MoE runs caller work beside its first dispatch (`DispatchOverlap`), and the block hands it the first shared expert's gate/up projections. Barriers order the remaining transports so that each has an expert or chunk GEMM beside it, in the forward and in the backward's recompute.
- Each layer's carry offload copy starts after the layer's weight slices. XLA puts the 4.3 ms carry copy and the slices on the same memcpy streams in program order, and without this ordering the weight prefetch lands a slice behind the copy and stalls the layer (98-152 ms/step on the production wheel). On #9708's head, disabling only this ordering slowed the step by 0.79%.

Configurations without the carry offload keep the plain path. Neither path is safe under XLA's default scheduler, which can start two transports together, so the launcher refuses a ragged carry-offload run whose XLA flags switch the latency-hiding scheduler off. `forward_barrier` is an `optimization_barrier` whose backward passes cotangents straight through, so a weight gradient's all-reduce and FSDP slice still fuse into a reduce-scatter.

In a four-GPU gate, loss and drop counts are bitwise unchanged and gradients change at rounding level, within the difference between two runs of the same code. In the hero the carry ordering also moves fusion boundaries, so its forward changes at rounding level.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [haliax] Add Pallas-Triton tile-map ragged_dot kernels for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
On AMD Instinct GPUs, `ragged_dot(..., implementation="triton")` now runs a second family of Pallas-Triton grouped-GEMM kernels, called tile-map kernels. NVIDIA GPUs, TPU and megablox behave exactly as before. NVIDIA keeps the existing group-grid kernels and block sizes, including the Blackwell `block_n` of 256. Those kernels are unchanged in the diff. `_TILE_MAP_GPU_FAMILIES` lists the GPU families that use the tile-map kernels. Adding NVIDIA to it is a one-line change, for a follow-up once H100 and B200 have been measured.

These kernels use Pallas-Triton, which JAX 0.11 deprecates; Mosaic GPU, the replacement JAX suggests, does not support ROCm. #9859 ports the same kernels to Triton launched through `jax_triton.triton_call`, but jax-triton kernels hang multi-GPU training on ROCm today. On a kernel's first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so when the 8 GPUs of one process launch together, all but one fail and the step stalls at the next collective (evidence in #9859). This PR lands the Pallas-Triton version so AMD runs can use the tile-map kernels now. #9859 replaces them once a jaxlib release fixes the race.

The existing kernels give every group a full grid over all row tiles and exit early on most of them. In the tile-map kernels, the forward and input-gradient (dlhs) kernels launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a tile map built on device from `group_sizes`, as in megablox's `make_group_metadata`. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. The weight gradient (drhs) uses one flat grid over all groups. Rows past `sum(group_sizes)` are zero-filled. The old kernels leave them unwritten. Block sizes come from a per-GPU-family table that was swept on MI350X. Two launch-order options are new: chiplet-aware program numbering (`num_xcds`) and grouped tile rows (`group_m`).

Per-call times on one MI350X, bf16, balanced groups. Each cell is TFLOP/s for the old kernels, then the new ones (job 453824). The June expert shapes are G=32, with w13 at K=N=2560 and w2 at K=1280, N=2560.

| Shape | M | fwd | dlhs | drhs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13 | 16384 | 94 → 594 | 88 → 635 | 378 → 483 |
| June w13 | 131072 | 587 → 730 | 556 → 808 | 428 → 585 |
| June w13 | 196608 | 525 → 735 | 511 → 818 | 429 → 579 |
| June w2 | 131072 | 560 → 668 | 541 → 765 | 403 → 586 |
| Mixtral-like w1, G=8, 4096x14336 | 16384 | 425 → 771 | 383 → 861 | 435 → 593 |
| Mixtral-like w1 | 65536 | 629 → 792 | 596 → 898 | 449 → 591 |

A dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs runs at about 730-960 TFLOP/s on this GPU. A sweep of `group_m` from 1 to 16 and `num_xcds` of 1 or 8 ran at both shape sets. Every setting beat the old kernels, and the chosen AMD entries are within 5% of the best setting sampled.

The full June model ran on 8x MI350X with EP8, `gpu_pallas_triton_flash` attention, memory fraction 0.90 and 20 steps. The table gives the median step over steps 2-19:

| Remat | Batch | Old kernels | New kernels | Peak memory (new) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| recompute_all | 64 | 2.149 s (122.0k tok/s) | 1.853 s (141.5k tok/s) | 158.4 GiB |
| recompute_all | 96 | 3.080 s (127.7k tok/s) | 2.696 s (145.9k tok/s) | 164.7 GiB |
| save_moe | 64 | 1.988 s (131.9k tok/s) | 1.832 s (143.1k tok/s) | 205.8 GiB |
| save_moe | 96 | 2.867 s (137.2k tok/s) | 2.672 s (147.2k tok/s) | 235.7 GiB |

Step-19 loss agrees with the old kernels within 1e-4. Earlier batch-96 runs on these kernels took 4.5-5.0 s per step, and one ran out of memory. Those runs reused XLA autotuning results from the per-fusion autotune cache, which JAX keeps inside `--compilation-cache-dir`. With that cache off (`JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`) or empty, batch 96 runs at 2.66-2.70 s and its throughput is above batch 64. The kernels were not the cause: per call they are 25-35% faster at batch 96's M=196608. With a warm autotune cache, save_moe at batch 64 took 4.95 s per step on the new kernels and 5.62 s on the old ones. With fresh autotuning it took 1.83 s and 1.99 s. Jobs: 453914, 453961 and 453944 (A/B), 453791 and 453823 (cache reproduction).

The per-call numbers and the block-size sweep came from `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which is in #9894. The edge-case tests (empty groups, unaligned boundaries, rows past the last group, partial tiles, every VJP layout) run for both families on a GPU. The tile-map family also runs them on CPU through the Pallas interpreter. Tests passed on MI350X (job 453882) and on the CPU interpreter (job 453881), and again after rebasing onto current main: all 72 on MI350X (job 458117), and on MI300X 42 passed with the 30 f32 cases skipped (job 458116). f32 cases skip on NVIDIA and on gfx942 (MI300X, MI325X), because Triton runs f32 dots in TF32 there. `test_accelerator_implementation_value_and_gradients_match_xla` now runs at highest matmul precision, as #9922 did for the custom VJP test: at default precision, XLA's autotuner on MI300X decides per process whether f32 dots run in xf32, and the test failed in 3 of 5 MI300X runs. With the change it passed 10 of 10 (job 458222).

topics.title: [grug] Fuse the expert dSwiGLU and skip recomputed pre-activation stores
topics.body:
Two changes to the routed experts' QuACK kernels, each bitwise or within bf16 rounding:

| Change | Kernel | Hero step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SwiGLU backward and the routing-weight row dot in the dh GEMM's epilogue | 3.54 ms against 5.10 ms per expert chunk | 13.059 to 12.943 s (+0.89%) |
| No gate/up pre-activation store in a forward whose residuals are recomputed | 6.14 ms against 6.48 ms per median chunk, 96 chunks per step | 12.652 to 12.611 s (+0.33%) |

The expert MLP backward wrote dh = dy @ W2^T to HBM and read it back with the gate/up pre-activations in an elementwise pass for the SwiGLU backward and the row dot <h, dh>. A QuACK epilogue on the grouped dh GEMM now unpacks the interleaved (gate, up) tile, applies the SwiGLU backward to the fp32 accumulator, writes the packed (d_gate, d_up) and reduces the row dot, so dh is never materialized. Outputs, drops and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; dx, dW13 and dS change at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp), because the SwiGLU backward runs on the unrounded accumulator.

Under the hero's layer remat, the forward's gated GEMM wrote the [C, 2I] pre-activations of every chunk, which the backward recomputes. `_routed_experts` declares `optimize_remat`, so such a forward runs a primal that calls the expert MLP's new `apply`, which returns the output alone, and the gated GEMM gains a launcher that never writes the pre-activations. Each chunk's dispatch still waits on the previous chunk's gate/up output. The forward is bitwise unchanged, and removing the change from all of #9708 slowed the step by 0.47%.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [inference] Reserve backend ports and verify served models
topics.body:
Allocate a task-owned Iris backend port to each direct and brokered inference worker. North Mini Code and Nemotron previously selected the same released ephemeral port on g1cbf32; North's 602 MRCR requests reached Nemotron. The incident is recorded at https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/662.

Require the configured served model in /v1/models before marking vLLM ready. A wrong-model response now fails startup with the advertised IDs.

Fixes #9862

topics.title: [iris] Give tasks a token that acts as the job's owner
topics.body:
Stacks on #9817.

A controller with auth enabled now mints a control-plane token for each
dispatched task, with the job's owner as subject and the new role "task". It
rides on RunTaskRequest.task_token, and the Docker worker and the Kubernetes
pod builder put it in IRIS_TASK_TOKEN for every profile except
CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX. The in-task client (iris_ctx, IrisClient.in_cluster,
ClusterResolver) presents it on every controller RPC.

Today a task reaches the controller only through auth.trusted_cidrs, which
makes it the anonymous admin. On every production cluster tasks share their
node's address, so those ranges cannot be narrowed while tasks have no other
credential. With the token, child-job submission, endpoint registration and
resolution, and ExecInContainer work under the owner's identity.

The task role has no admin authority. A task may give a child job an elevated
container profile or the PRODUCTION or SYSTEM band only when the child's
parent already holds it, so existing privileged and production job trees keep
launching children. Raw SQL queries and budget changes fail for a task that
presents its token, and a root job a task submits is owned by the job's owner.
Each dispatch mints a fresh token, valid for 30 days and not revocable. Under
null auth no token is minted. On Kubernetes the token is a plain env value in
the pod spec, readable by anyone who can read pods in the Iris namespace.

This change does not narrow auth.trusted_cidrs, so a task that drops its token
is still the anonymous admin. The proposed per-cluster values are in the issue,
not in this change; they need this change deployed first, and on GCP and
CoreWeave the node ranges they keep still include every non-sandbox task.

Part of #9816

topics.title: [tpu-inference] Qwen3.5 hybrid GDN prefill ~10x slower than pure attention on v6e
topics.body:
Serving Qwen3.5-9B (hybrid GDN attention, `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`) on v6e-8 at fork main (`e8809d49`), prefill runs at ~6-7k prompt tokens/s through the `chunked_jax_pd` kernel — roughly 10x slower than Qwen3-8B's pure-attention prefill on the same slice. The engine sits at ~2 running requests with KV cache 0.1% used, so the batch is kernel-compute-bound, not budget- or memory-bound; raising `max_num_batched_tokens` 512 -> 2048 changed neither throughput nor concurrency.

Observed impact: a full 5-shot MMLU (56k echo+prompt-logprobs requests) takes ~3.2h for Qwen3.5-9B vs ~3-10 minutes for Qwen3-8B on identical hardware and pins. Decode throughput looks unremarkable; the gap is prefill.

Repro: serve `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B` on v6e-8 (defaults, tensor_parallel per the sizing heuristic), then drive prompt-heavy traffic, e.g. lm-eval `local-completions` MMLU with `echo=True` + prompt logprobs at concurrency 16. Watch prefill tokens/s in the engine stats.

Marin-side context: marin-community/marin#7345 (eval system) — the Qwen3.5-9B column of the eval grid pays this cost on every MMLU-class run.

topics.title: [iris] Follow re-registered serve endpoints from Evalchemy evals
topics.body:
Evalchemy children now reach their serve through a loopback relay that looks
the endpoint name up in the Iris registry, instead of a host:port resolved once
at launch. When Kueue preempts the serve and its retry registers on another
host, the old address refuses connections, hangs, or answers 404. The eval used
to retry that address until the group timed out: nine groups on cw-rno2a were
lost this way on 2026-10-09/10, some after 16-20 h.

The relay (iris.cluster.client.endpoint_relay) looks the name up every 30 s and
after each connection failure or 404. It aborts requests still waiting on a
replaced address and replays requests that have no response yet once the
endpoint is registered again (for up to 1 h, then 503). A response that has
started is never replayed; the relay drops the client connection so lm-eval's
own retries apply. Each relay thread keeps a pooled direct connection, so evals
keep the direct routing that #9480 chose over the hub proxy.

The fix sits in an Iris client module so any in-cluster client can use it. A
stable cluster-level address (a per-endpoint Kubernetes Service, or
controller-side forwarding) would cover every client without a helper process,
but it needs a controller deploy and work in each backend. The hub proxy
already follows re-registrations, and it is the path #9480 moved away from. The
relay ships in the job bundle and takes effect on the next eval launch.

While the Evalchemy job runs, the parent now reads the serve job states every
60 s. When one is terminal, it cancels the Evalchemy job and the record becomes
infra_failed with the serve job ID and state. A failed status read does not end
the eval. Before, the parent waited with no bound.

Tests drive the relay with real HTTP servers and a fake registry whose endpoint
moves mid-run. On a local in-process Iris cluster, the relay CLI in a client
task followed a serve job that was cancelled and replaced under the same
endpoint name; the request in flight during the gap waited about 4 s and was
answered by the replacement. Not yet run on CoreWeave: the registry lookup with
a task token (the local cluster has no auth) and starting the relay from
$IRIS_VENV inside a real Evalchemy child.

Fixes #10030

topics.title: [grug] Add GB200 launch and H100 validation support
topics.body:
Stack the GB200 launcher, checkpoint/data support and H100 validation runner on the pipeline foundation in #9279 for the model recipe from main `89ac0d770506f7e27ca217760ec5ca3246694e7e`. The launcher uses FP32 parameters, BF16 compute, compute-scaled MuonH, SM100 ragged transport and Flash Attention. It requests one hard NVLink domain in the opportunistic BATCH queue and separates queue wait from worker execution deadlines. Future run names use `pipeline-gb200-*` or `pipeline-h100-*`.

Executable `0da04acccf7b0842319a8668d71ccc697a7b10ec` completed the corrected eight-GB200 synthetic gate with two full-width layers, PP2/EP4 and sequence length 4096. The two losses were 11.806337356567383 and 0.4912489652633667. All eight native GPU processes, both Iris GPU tasks and the coordinator exited zero. All 48 startup task ABI records had zero input memory-kind mismatches. Both coordinator failure and preemption retry caps were zero; the SDK launch example sets both explicitly because the CLI retry option controls failure retries only. [GB200 setup and standalone commands](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/experiments/grug/moe_hero_pipeline/GB200.md) record prerequisites and acceptance criteria.

The combined H100 runner was validated at `a1e3ab278eeb05bb645db641dd3e7dabedf90dbb` on 16 H100s with two full-width layers, PP2/EP8 and sequence length 4096. Ten synthetic updates had finite losses from 11.804966926574707 to 0.4793720245361328. Twenty fresh Harrier updates consumed 2,621,440 tokens with finite losses from 11.8075590133667 to 7.612007141113281. All 200 raw components remained nonempty with their original mixture weights and order. Both GPU tasks and supervisors exited zero; fresh-data logs retain 15 individual rank exits, while the supervisor's child-reaping contract certifies all 16. No checkpoint was written in those full-width trials. Save/restore support is included, but hardware checkpoint validation is limited to the historical reduced-model comparison: a 90,018,826-byte scratch checkpoint and a resumed-versus-uninterrupted loss difference of 9.5367431640625e-7, within unchanged 1e-5 tolerances. The current full-width main-recipe checkpoint path has not been validated on GPUs. These runs used the explicit SM90 pooled-wave/FA4 adapter with SYRK disabled and establish no H100 ragged-transport parity. [H100 reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/docs/references/hero-pipeline-h100.md) separates these runs from the historical reduced-model checkpoint comparison.

The runtime pins upstream JAXPP `328f75a80cecf22c7cc030a82d8941d3c1e220b6` plus a tracked host-memory/startup overlay. JAX 0.11.1 overrides JAXPP's declared compatibility cap and remains experimental; CUDA dependencies with lower bounds are recorded per launch. Installer recovery avoids duplicate global reinstall flags, including on deployed older worker wrappers. The [Iris installer incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/600) distinguishes the initiating GitHub fetch failure from the broken recovery command. Main-recipe argument parsing rejects AdamW before distributed initialization. Shared pipeline configuration, process ownership, array predicates, data scheduling and loader cleanup consolidate the overlapping work from #9279 and #9460.

#9279 contains the shared expert-bank normalization correction, FP32 main-recipe precision and optional frozen QB bias, together with their CPU regressions and historical layout explanation. The hardware gates used FP32 parameters and BF16 compute, with per-expert normalization and adaptive QB. They do not validate the shared-bank normalization correction or frozen-QB mode.

The combined executable, runtime and test source is identical to the previously published `5c2d91a6e48a43573b7f0b09be7e5f16bfc3eddc` snapshot. The README now selects per-expert normalization explicitly in its historical reproduction command. Required lint, type checks, hooks, strict docs and source-link checks passed on that source. The affected safe suite passed 5,566 tests with 18 skips and six expected failures, using library imports from the current checkout. Focused CPU coverage passed 81 tests; the previous normalization fails the new layout regression. The committed-branch lint-catalog review completed; the new error-wording assertion finding was fixed. Before merge, #9279 owns the named compiled-initializer result, repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers and synthetic runner lifecycle cleanup. This extension then owns adapting its checkpoint/data lifecycle. Those deferred changes need compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation.

Full 48-layer main-recipe execution remains unvalidated. The 64-GB200 rack attempt acquired its allocation and started some native processes, then failed during runtime installation; it produced no finite training updates. The full 192-H100/48-layer/65K run remains held. This pull request remains draft.

topics.title: [haliax] Add tile-map Triton ragged_dot kernels for AMD Instinct GPUs
topics.body:
Do not merge yet: on ROCm, jaxlib 0.11.1 races when the GPUs of one process first launch the same jax-triton kernel, and an 8-GPU training step with these kernels hangs at its first collective. The cause and evidence are below; merging waits for a jaxlib fix. Until then, #10009 lands the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels, and this PR replaces it.

On AMD Instinct GPUs, `ragged_dot(..., implementation="triton")` now runs a second family of grouped-GEMM kernels, called tile-map kernels, written in Triton and launched through `jax_triton.triton_call` as Grug's routing top-k (#9942) is. JAX 0.11 deprecates the Pallas-Triton backend, and Mosaic GPU, the replacement JAX suggests, does not support ROCm. AMD Instinct GPUs use the tile-map kernels when jax-triton imports, which on ROCm needs jaxlib 0.11.1, and fall back to the group-grid kernels otherwise. NVIDIA GPUs, TPU and megablox behave exactly as before. NVIDIA keeps the existing Pallas-Triton group-grid kernels and block sizes, including the Blackwell `block_n` of 256. `_TILE_MAP_GPU_FAMILIES` lists the GPU families that use the tile-map kernels. Adding NVIDIA to it is a one-line change, for a follow-up once H100 and B200 have been measured.

The existing kernels give every group a full grid over all row tiles and exit early on most of them. In the tile-map kernels, the forward and input-gradient (dlhs) kernels launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a tile map built on device from `group_sizes`, as in megablox's `make_group_metadata`. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. The weight gradient (drhs) uses one flat grid over all groups and reads its lhs tile transposed. Rows past `sum(group_sizes)` are zero-filled. The old kernels leave them unwritten. Block sizes come from a per-GPU-family table swept on MI350X. Two launch-order options are new: chiplet-aware program numbering (`num_xcds`) and grouped tile rows (`group_m`).

Per-call times on one MI350X, bf16, balanced groups. Each cell is TFLOP/s for the old kernels, then the new ones (job 457866). The June expert shapes are G=32, with w13 at K=N=2560 and w2 at K=1280, N=2560.

| Shape | M | fwd | dlhs | drhs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13 | 16384 | 95 → 621 | 88 → 632 | 382 → 506 |
| June w13 | 131072 | 598 → 784 | 570 → 806 | 433 → 689 |
| June w13 | 196608 | 542 → 800 | 526 → 826 | 435 → 707 |
| June w2 | 131072 | 569 → 725 | 555 → 764 | 415 → 639 |
| Mixtral-like w1, G=8, 4096x14336 | 16384 | 423 → 815 | 383 → 864 | 443 → 756 |
| Mixtral-like w1 | 65536 | 633 → 857 | 601 → 907 | 457 → 777 |

A dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs runs at about 730-960 TFLOP/s on this GPU.

An earlier revision of this PR wrote the tile-map kernels in Pallas-Triton. At every shape above, the jax-triton kernels return outputs bitwise identical to that version on MI350X and MI300X (jobs 457866, 457867). XLA compiles Pallas-Triton kernels with its bundled Triton, while jax-triton uses pip triton 3.6, and with the same block config the jax-triton drhs kernel ran 29-33% slower on MI350X. Reading the lhs tile transposed and a new drhs sweep (job 457862) fixed that: 256x256x64 blocks with 8 warps and 2 stages reach at least 94% of the best of 272 configurations at each of five shapes. Against the Pallas-Triton version, drhs now runs 4-30% faster on MI350X and 31-76% faster on MI300X, fwd 2-8% faster and dlhs up to 2% slower on MI350X, and fwd and dlhs within 3% on MI300X. The fwd and dlhs entries are the ones swept with the Pallas-Triton version.

On ROCm, jax-triton hands jaxlib the path of a temporary hsaco file. On a kernel's first launch, `GetModuleImage` in `jaxlib/gpu/triton_kernels.cc` misses its cache, then reads the file and deletes it without holding its lock. When the 8 device threads of one process launch a new kernel together, all but one fail with `/tmp/tmp...; No such file or directory` and skip the rest of the step, and the others wait at the next collective until XLA aborts. In the June model on 8x MI350X with EP8, recompute_all and batch 64, any one of the three layouts on jax-triton triggers it (job 457945). A gdb breakpoint on `XlaCustomCallStatusSetFailure` caught the error (job 457957), and strace showed the 8 threads unlinking the same file within 0.3 ms (job 457961). Other jax-triton kernels in multi-GPU ROCm runs hit the same race, including #9942's top-k. The fix belongs in jaxlib: compile under the lock, or stop deleting the file. With the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels, the same step took 2.420 s against 2.627 s with the group-grid kernels (job 457874, reference attention).

The edge-case tests (empty groups, unaligned boundaries, rows past the last group, partial tiles, every VJP layout) run for both families on a GPU. All 88 pass on MI350X (job 457875). On MI300X, 58 pass and the 30 f32 cases skip, because Triton runs f32 dots in TF32 on gfx942 as it does on NVIDIA (job 457876). The tile-map kernels no longer run on CPU, so a CPU test checks that the tile map assigns every row to exactly one tile of its group. The per-call numbers and block sweeps come from `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which is in #9894, stacked on this PR.

Background and earlier measurements: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027367267

Part of #9812

topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

topics.title: [post-training] Transfer two Snowball experts at once: MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS and weight merging
topics.body:
Follow-up to #9920 (single-expert transfer: plain SFT, RS-SFT and OPD each moved the CruxEval expert E's gain back into the Snowball student B). Design note is kept by the owner; this issue is the summary and coordination record.

**TL;DR.** Build a second expert E_2 from B the same way as E, in a different domain (MMLU-Pro), then compare four ways of putting both experts' gains into B at once: multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD from E + E_2), SFT on mixed demos, SFT on rejection-sampled mixed demos, and weight merging of B + E + E_2. Every arm is scored on both domains, so the design also measures forgetting (the domain an arm was not trained for) and collapse (GSM8K, GPQA-D, MATH500). Status: data for E_2 prepared and verified; E_2 training awaits approval; no arm has run.

**Questions.**
1. Do the experts themselves collapse in the other domain after GLM SFT? (E on MMLU-Pro and GPQA-D; E_2 on CruxEval; both on GSM8K.)
2. When both experts are transferred into B at once, how much of each domain is recovered and how much of the other is lost?
3. How do MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS and merging compare on that, and at what cost?

**Models.** B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5` (unchanged). E = the #9920 CruxEval expert (`…/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`; CruxEval 79.4 / 71.4 vs B 55.4 / 57.8; GPQA-D 44.8% vs B 41.9%, 198 questions × 3 repeats, no observed drop). E_2 = B + full SFT on GLM 5.3 MMLU-Pro traces with E's exact recipe: AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3% warmup then cosine, 3 epochs, fresh optimizer state, frozen router bias, 32 H100.

**E_2 domain and data.** MMLU-Pro (B 44.1%, GLM 5.3 85.8% under the frozen evaluator). The GLM trace collection had indexed the dataset by question text; 200 questions appear in 2–3 prompt variants, so 190 docs carried a wrong gold letter and 175 GLM grades flipped. Every captured doc was re-joined to the pinned dataset (TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro test @ `b189ec765aa7ed75c8acfea42df31fdae71f97be`) by exact question + ordered options and relabelled; B's stored per-doc labels were independently correct (5,303/12,032 = 44.07% under both label sets). Training subset: a seeded, category-proportional draw of whole question groups (every prompt variant of a picked question travels with it): 1,589 questions = 1,606 docs, 1,359 with a usable GLM trace (correct, finished, reasoning present, fits 32,768 tokens under B's template); 729,901 supervised tokens per epoch. Docs without a usable trace stay in the subset denominator untrained. The other 10,426 docs are held out from this fine-tuning and scored as a probe. B on the subset 43.9%, on the remainder 44.1%; GLM 85.7% / 85.9%. Artifacts (SHA-pinned, independently verified): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/`.

**E_2 gate (operational).** Paired gain over B on the subset ≥ 10 pp as a point estimate and lower 95% group-bootstrap bound ≥ 5 pp on the first pass; if the first pass lands in [8, 10) on the gain or [3, 5) on the bound, one second pass is run and the gate is re-evaluated on both passes pooled (never the better pass). GSM8K paired drop over 2 pp stops the arm. CruxEval, GPQA-D, MATH500 and the held-out score are reported, not gated.

**Frozen evaluator.** As #9920: Evalchemy `c131e5ab`, vLLM H100x8 DP8+EP8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap (28,672 for GPQA-D), thinking on, temperature 1.0 unseeded. MMLU-Pro runs always score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record against the canonical labels, with bootstrap intervals that resample question groups.

**Arms (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the same 3,206 prompts = 1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro; one checkpoint per epoch).**
- MOPD from E + E_2: 4 rollouts per prompt, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (MarinSkyRL routed teachers), one teacher node each.
- Mixed SFT: one demo per prompt (E's sample 0 from the #9920 k=8 CruxEval pool; E_2's sample 0 from a new k=8 collection on the 1,606), the SFT counterpart of MOPD on the same prompts and epochs (prompt-matched, not token-matched).
- Mixed SFT-RS: first execution-correct (CruxEval) or answer-correct (MMLU-Pro) sample per prompt from the two k=8 pools; uncovered prompts stay in the denominators. Uses verifier access the other arms do not have.
- Merge B + E + E_2: #9974 tools with B as anchor and E, E_2 as donors, task arithmetic B + a·(E−B) + b·(E_2−B) over a small coefficient grid plus TIES and DARE-TIES; CPU only, no training.
- Dropped: OPD from E_2 alone and plain SFT from E_2 demos alone (the single-expert question was answered in #9920).

**Selection and reporting.** As #9920: prefer the final checkpoint when it is similar or better on every target metric (similar = paired 95% CI includes 0, an operational threshold); otherwise a second pass on the last two checkpoints and the two-pass means decide. Costs in H100-hours from Iris task durations (method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298); full-run figures labelled as such; demo generation counted once; failed-eval overhead separate. One consolidated final comment; no running log here.

**Budget (planning estimates).** E_2 ≈ 30–40 H100-h; k=8 E_2 demos on 1,606 prompts ≈ 2; MOPD ≈ 300–500 (7 nodes; set by the smoke run); mixed SFT and SFT-RS ≈ 60–120 each; merge CPU only; evaluations ≈ 150.

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-09: MMLU-Pro chosen as E_2's domain (GPQA-D too small to train on: 198 questions). Subset = whole question groups, ~1,600 docs; remainder held out as a probe. GLM labels repaired and verified by two agents; B labels confirmed. Arms fixed to MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merge(B,E,E_2); OPD-from-E_2 and E_2-only SFT dropped. New issue opened rather than continuing in #9920.

comments.body: 🤖 Decision log, 2026-10-10 21:10 UTC: owner reduced the MOPD(E+E_2) run to 2 epochs (≈102 updates, 7 H100x8 nodes) after the smoke run measured ≈9.6 min per update, about twice the single-teacher OPD run; projected ≈900 H100-h instead of ≈1,800 for 4 epochs. Smoke gate passed (exact 1:1 routing, both teachers scoring, finite advantages, export and router biases verified). Full run submitted 21:07 UTC. Merge arm: three B+E+E_2 checkpoints built on CPU (task arithmetic 1.0/1.0 and 0.5/0.5, TIES density 0.5; router biases exactly equal to B); their first MATH500 records are invalid (Evalchemy per-request timeouts), and the 1.0/1.0 merge shows runaway generations (IFEval p90 output length 103k characters vs B 0.7k); evaluation continues staggered. E_2 MMLU-Pro subset curve: 57.2 (epoch 1) → 64.1 → 66.4 (final, selected). k=8 E_2 demo collection done (8.9 H100-h); mixed-SFT arms launch after its audit.

topics.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
topics.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

topics.title: [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend
topics.body:
This is the top of a three-PR stack. The two PRs below it prepare `ep_ring.py` so this backend can share ring's gather helpers and local assignment selection instead of copying them.

Add `ring_dedup`, an opt-in expert-parallel MoE backend selected with `moe_implementation="ring_dedup"`. `ring` all-gathers every token to every expert shard and reduce-scatters a full-size output. With top-4 of 256 experts over 8 shards, a token reaches 3.3 shards on average, so most of those bytes go to shards that do no work on them.

`ring_dedup` sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its top-4 experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`. A small metadata `all_to_all` carries the combine weights and local expert ids, and a trailer row holds the sender's valid count. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule and the Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32, and returns one row per token. Every hidden-width movement is a gather, so neither pass uses a scatter-add.

The sender capacity per destination is `pooled_transport_capacity_factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing, and `moe_mlp` raises if it is unset. It reuses the `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` parameter so one benchmark flag sets the sender capacity for both backends. The June benchmark sets it with `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` from #9852; 1.1 gave no sender drops. At batch 64 each collective moves 537 MB per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring.

On CPU in f32, the 8-shard tests match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in outputs and gradients, including forced sender drops. At full shapes in bf16 the output differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative, because `ring_dedup` sums in f32. The drop rate is 1.00-1.12%, against 0.93-0.99% for ring.

June Snowball 67B-A2B, 8x MI350X, EP8, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile caches:

| Remat | ring | ring_dedup | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.730 s (13.07% MFU) | 1.580 s (14.31% MFU) | 454012 / 454021 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.798 s | 1.688 s | 454022 / 454026 |

One `ring_dedup` run (job 454010) ran out of memory on GPU 7 at step 5 and hung; its retry passed. That was allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer, which also hits ring at batch 96, and #9901 fixes it with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` in the HPC Fund wrapper. We have not measured `ring_dedup` on TPU or NVIDIA.

Stack, in merge order (each PR is based on the one before):
1. #9860 [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for ROCm (base `main`). Adds the gather helpers `_dispatch_rows` and `_combine_rows` that this backend reuses.
2. #9928 [grug] Move ring's local assignment selection into a helper (base `grug/rocm-ring-combine-top-k`, #9860's branch). Adds `_select_local_assignments`, which this backend calls.
3. #9880 this PR (base `grug/ring-select-local-assignments`, #9928's branch).

The timings above were measured with the ROCm routing top-k from #9889 in place. That kernel is not needed here and is being replaced by #9942. The ring column ran ring with the gather combine, which #9860 now selects with `moe_implementation="ring_gather_combine"`.

Part of #9812

topics.title: FP8 loss-curve validation: bf16 (main) vs FP8 (PR #7079) at row-13 scale on 64x H100
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment validated the FP8 changes from PR #7079 against a bf16 control at the row-13 Grug MoE scale, using identical seed and data order and a full 24,000-step schedule on H100s. After smoke debugging reduced the run to one 8-H100 node per arm and fixed allocator fragmentation with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, both arms completed cleanly. The loss-curve gate passed: FP8 ended with a matched-step gap of about +0.0040, flat through the cooldown tail and inside the <=0.01 acceptance bar, while running about 5.5% faster by throughput. The campaign also found two follow-ups that do not block the gate: BFC allocator fragmentation can silently deadlock training collectives without `cuda_async`, and FP8 currently uses about 1.66x the bf16 transient step arena because XLA keeps cast/transpose FP8 operands resident for backward GEMMs.

### Helpful links
- [Final result comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7298#issuecomment-5010209991)
- [W&B overlay group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/fp8-loss-val-7079)
- [Final comparison artifact](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Part of #6699. Validates PR #7079 (FP8 expert GEMMs + FP8 EP wire + FP8 dense GEMMs for attention/shared-expert) against a bf16 control on real data — the loss-curve gate flagged in the PR before FP8 defaults can flip.

**Motivation:** before FP8 can become a default, we need evidence that enabling it does not perturb the training loss at production scale. This experiment runs a bf16 control (main) and an FP8 test arm (PR #7079) in parallel on the CoreWeave H100s from identical init and data order, saving the full per-step loss trajectory for both, and compares them. The run is sized (~8 h, cached in-cluster dataset, full LR schedule) to show substantial loss movement while resolving 0.01-level precision deltas — using the cluster-resident SlimPajama cache to avoid cross-region data costs and staying within a 64-H100 budget.

## Design

Two arms in parallel on cw-us-east-02a, 4 nodes / 32 H100 each (64 total):

| arm | code | precision |
|---|---|---|
| `fp8val-bf16-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val-ctl` = main + launcher | bf16 |
| `fp8val-fp8-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val` = PR #7079 merged with main + launcher | `GrugFp8Config(wire=True, dense=True)` |

- **Model:** row-13 flagship shape — d2560, 26 layers, 64 experts top-4 (+shared), MHA 20×128, seq 4096, sliding window 2048, qk_mult 1.3, ~18B params; `ring` MoE backend, EP8 intra-node, FSDP over 4 nodes, `gpu_fa4_cute` attention, `recompute_all` remat. Identical in both arms; seed 0 in both (same init + data order).
- **Optimizer:** production MuonH (`lr=1e-3`, `adam_lr=1e-4`, warmup 10%, cooldown to 0) run through the **full schedule** — #6486 showed precision gaps surface in the cooldown tail, so a truncated schedule can show false parity.
- **Data:** SlimPajama-6B llama3-tokenized cache already materialized under this cluster's `MARIN_PREFIX` (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin`, in-cluster LOTA endpoint) — zero cross-region traffic. Feistel block shuffle.
- **Budget:** ~11k steps × 128 seqs × 4096 tok ≈ 5.8B tokens/arm, sized from measured H100 throughput to finish inside ~8 h (final step count calibrated by a short smoke run). Precedent: #6486 resolved 0.01-level loss deltas at 1.4B tokens.
- **Trajectory:** W&B project `marin_moe`, group `fp8-loss-val-7079`, `log_every=1` (per-step `train/loss`).

**Acceptance:** matched-step train-loss overlay; gap ≤0.01 at end of schedule (the #6486 threshold for a meaningful difference), with specific attention to the last 10% (cooldown tail). Divergence, NaNs, or a growing gap fails the gate.

Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` on `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val`.

Note: not filed under the #4281 recipe-ablation family — this is infra/precision validation for #6699, not a recipe-change experiment.

topics.title: [zephyr] Abort ThreadedBatchWriter output when the producer fails
topics.body:
When the body of a ThreadedBatchWriter `with` block raised, `__exit__` sent
the normal end-of-stream sentinel. The write function then completed, and
`write_parquet_file` committed the partial file through `atomic_rename`.
Stages that treat an existing output file as "shard done" then skipped the
shard on a re-run and kept the partial output. The normalize main/dups writer
and the datakit quality writer use this pattern.

`__exit__` now sets an abort event before it wakes the thread. The next read
of the write function's stream raises `WriterAbortedError`, so `atomic_rename`
removes its temporary file and nothing is committed. A normal close is
unchanged.

The datakit quality stage in #9694 removes partial outputs after the fact
(`_discard_outputs`); with this change, that code is not necessary.

topics.title: [iris] Renew worker credentials before expiry
topics.body:
Renew worker credentials one day before their 30-day expiry, including while workers are idle, and persist replacements across process restarts. Restrict renewal to authenticated workers and admins; expired credentials still require operator recovery. Controllers refresh provisioning credentials, and manual worker creation and restart obtain fresh tokens from the controller.

An expired worker token could remain unnoticed while the log client reused a cached Finelog endpoint. After a timeout invalidated that cache, controller endpoint discovery rejected the token and log batches were discarded even though tasks continued running. The October 9 audit found expired credentials on six CPU workers; targeted credential replacement and process restarts restored central logging without restarting their seven task containers.

Deploy the controller renewal RPC before the worker changes. Worker tokens remain shared identities without individual revocation; a stolen token can also renew itself.

[Incident diagnosis and recovery](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/691).

topics.title: [haliax] Tune tile-map ragged_dot dlhs and drhs blocks for MI300X
topics.body:
Give MI300X and MI325X (gfx942) their own dlhs and drhs tile-map blocks for the Triton `ragged_dot` kernels: 128x256x32, 4 warps, 8 XCDs, group_m=2, with 2 pipeline stages for dlhs and 1 for drhs. Until now gfx942 reused the MI350X (gfx950) blocks. gfx942 has 64 KiB of LDS per CU, against 160 KiB on gfx950, and the MI350X dlhs and drhs blocks run 20-35% slower on MI300X than the swept tile. The forward pass keeps the MI350X block (256x256x64). 128x256x32 is 16% faster for fwd at the June shape with M=16384, but no faster at M=131072 and 15-22% slower at a Mixtral-like shape.

The table is keyed on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` from #9904. That PR makes `implementation="auto"` prefer XLA on gfx942, so these blocks apply when Triton is selected explicitly. Merge order: #10009, then #9904, then this PR.

The f32 skip in `test_triton_kernel_families_match_ragged_dot_general`, which #10009 adds for gfx942, now keys on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942`. Triton uses xf32 for f32 dots on gfx942, and the group-grid f32 tiles exceed the 64 KiB LDS.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X (partition `mi3001x`; jobs 454650, 454673, 454679 and 454683; sweeps 454658, 454659, 454667 and 454668) show that the tuned dlhs and drhs blocks cut a fwd+dlhs+drhs triple by 9-24%. For example, the June w13 shape at M=131072 drops from 14.67 ms to 12.25 ms.

At this branch's head, `lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py` gives 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223) and, on MI300X, 46 passed and 30 skipped (job 458222).

Part of #9812

topics.title: [datakit] Score quality from the tokenize stage's token ids
topics.body:
* Score quality from the tokenize stage's stored `input_ids`, with the classifier trained on `marin-community/marin-tokenizer`
* Regroup chunk rows and average begin/middle/end windows of 512 token ids; read document ids and sample text from normalize in lockstep
* Encode labels through the same per-record encoder, including special tokens; refuse a different tokenizer or normalize source before scoring
* Preserve output basenames, document order, and sample text; failed shards leave no completed output and permit retry
* Retrain `pooled_junkgate2_marin` on 5,578 oracle labels at `60bf2d0b79b6bfd3d41a3ab439ce5d5765735580`, with seed 0 and 796 reserved rows
  * Leading-window holdout AUC / Spearman: 0.8368 / 0.7150; begin/middle/end: 0.8350 / 0.7153
  * Deployed e5 scores on the same rows: 0.9205 / 0.8412 for begin/middle/end; its original training split is unverified
  * Begin/middle/end agreement with e5 across all labels: Spearman 0.8929, 67.84% identical buckets, and 99.03% within one bucket

topics.title: [eval] Iris retries overwrite completed run records
topics.body:
An Iris retry can reuse an evaluation's serialized `EvaluationIdentity.run_id` and `output_dir`. The replayed Evalchemy process then appends samples and overwrites `record.json` under an already sealed result URI. A tracker link can therefore change its score after it has been sealed.

Reproduce:
1. Submit an evaluation batch through `experiments/evaluation/launch.py` and let an Evalchemy process finish and seal its FineStore archive.
2. Cause Iris to classify the parent task or Evalchemy child task as retryable after that write, such as a post-completion `PodDeleted` or worker preemption.
3. Observe that the replay has a new Iris attempt or child-job ID but writes to the original FineStore path and run-level `record.json`.
4. Compare the first completed attempt, replayed attempt, and current record at that URI.

Expected: an Iris retry must preserve completed results as immutable artifacts. It should either skip a successfully sealed evaluation or allocate attempt-specific run IDs and output paths. A later failed attempt must not downgrade or replace an earlier succeeded record.

Confirmed examples:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-210313-Aleph-Alpha-Kolibri-1-mbppplus-b75b/results` first completed at 262/378 (`0.6931216931`). A parent-task retry ran a second MBPP+ child against a new serving endpoint and wrote 274/378 (`0.7248677249`) to the same path. The current `record.json` and FineStore view report the second score.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261002-002728-laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203-gpqa-diamond-5b7b/results` changed from `0.636` to `0.5993265993` after a parent `WORKER_FAILED` retry replayed GPQA-Diamond against a new serving child.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-nupa-9a91/results` held a sealed 5,000-item attempt with 2,414 correct answers (`0.4828`). Iris classified the completed Evalchemy child attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted`, retried the same task and path, and the final canonical record became `0.4788`.
- The Kolibri retry also changed MATH500 from `0.984` to `0.992` and HumanEval+ from `0.774` to `0.7682926829` under unchanged result URIs. When the retried parent was later killed, several earlier succeeded Kolibri `record.json` files were rewritten as `infra_failed`.

`_run_id()` is evaluated while constructing the batch in `experiments/evaluation/launch.py`; Iris retries replay the serialized batch. `write_record()` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py` then writes unconditionally to `{prefix}/{run_id}/record.json`.

topics.title: [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for ROCm
topics.body:
Add a `ring_gather_combine` MoE implementation: the ring expert-parallel backend with its dispatch and combine done as gathers in both directions. `ring` keeps the scatter-add combine, and `implementation=None` still resolves to `ring` on every platform. ROCm runs opt in with `moe_implementation="ring_gather_combine"`. Like the other expert-parallel implementations, it runs only on an expert mesh axis of size two or more. Without one, `moe_mlp` falls back to the local `scatter` path, so a single-device call never reaches the gather code.

On AMD GPUs the combine `zeros_like(x_global).at[token_local].add(...)` and the transpose of the dispatch `jnp.take` compile to scatter-adds that run at about 0.8-1.2 TB/s. `ring_gather_combine` builds an inverse map from each (token, k) assignment to the dispatch slot that holds it. The dispatch take and the combine get custom VJPs, so activation rows move only by gather in both directions: each token sums its at most K slot rows (K = 4 in the June model). The inverse map itself is an int32 scatter-set (`ep_common._assignment_sources`, 0.04 ms at June shapes), and the routing-weight gradient still scatter-adds one scalar per slot, as in `ring`. `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local` takes the dispatch and combine pair as an argument, and `moe_mlp` binds it when it picks the backend, so the ring code has no platform check. The combine's profile scope is renamed from `scatter` to `combine`, the name the other EP backends use.

In bf16 the two backends round differently. `ring_gather_combine` sums each token's rows in f32 and rounds to bf16 once, in the combine and in the dispatch gradient. `ring`'s bf16 scatter-add rounds after every add, on CPU and on MI300X, so the two can differ in the last bits of a token's sum. A bf16 test checks the gather sums bit for bit against an f32 sum rounded once, on inputs whose products and f32 sums are exact. On CPU the test fails if the sums run in bf16. On MI300X it cannot catch that, because XLA on ROCm keeps the fused bf16 sum in f32. At June shapes on one MI350X (job 453908), the combine matched an f32 scatter-add rounded to bf16 bit for bit. The order of a scatter-add's f32 adds is unspecified, so other inputs can differ in the last bit.

`ring` traces to the same program as on the merge base. Exporting its forward and backward for CUDA (8-way expert parallelism, bf16) gives an identical jaxpr and debug-stripped StableHLO with the XLA `ragged_dot`, and an identical jaxpr with the Triton `ragged_dot` that H100 uses by default. Pallas Triton cannot be lowered without a GPU, so that path was compared at the jaxpr level only. The profile scope name is the only difference.

The measurements below ran on an earlier revision that chose the gather path with a ROCm check inside `ep_ring.py`. The gather code is unchanged, except that the inverse map now comes from `_assignment_sources`, which runs the same scatter-set.

Single-MI350X microbenchmark at June per-GPU shapes (`bench_grug_ring_combine_top_k.py` from #9891, job 453908):

| | scatter-add | gather |
|---|---|---|
| combine forward | 2.420 ms | 0.969 ms |
| dispatch + combine, forward and backward | 5.436 ms | 1.790 ms |

Full June model, batch 64, flash attention, 8x MI350X, fresh compiles, step time with the gather path and the routing top-k from #9889 together:

| remat policy | before | after | jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.823 s (12.40% MFU) | 1.735 s (13.03% MFU) | 453972 / 453979 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.848 s | 1.788 s | 453841 / 453957 |

Losses agree within 4e-4. These runs used the flash attention from #9853 and the tuned Triton `ragged_dot` from #9859. This PR does not depend on either.

The ring tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py`, including `ring_gather_combine` against `ring` with capacity drops, pass on 8x MI300X (12 tests) and on CPU (9 tests; 3 in-process multi-device tests skip) in job 456128. The bf16 test and the other `ring_gather_combine` tests pass on 8x MI300X and on CPU in job 458228. With #9928 and #9880 stacked on top, the 17 ring tests pass on 8x MI300X in job 456022. Some MI300X runs hang in `test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[all_valid-ring]`, with one GPU busy and the other seven idle. The same test hangs on `main` (job 456135: 2 of 4 runs on this branch, 1 of 4 on `main`). On 8x MI350X (job 454059) the earlier revision passed the whole file except 5 ragged all-to-all tests, which also fail on `main` (job 454060) because `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` cannot parse `gfx950` as a compute capability. `ring_gather_combine` has not been measured on TPU or NVIDIA.

#9928 and then #9880 (`ring_dedup`) are stacked on this branch. `ring_dedup` reuses `_dispatch_rows` and `_combine_rows`.

topics.title: [inference] Eval runner keeps a stale serve endpoint after the serve job is preempted
topics.body:
When an Iris serve job started by `marin.inference.iris.remote_inference` (`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py`, `_start_direct_inference` / `_wait_for_endpoint`) is preempted by Kueue and its retry attempt registers a new endpoint on another host, the running evaluation keeps the first host:port it resolved. The Evalchemy chat client then loops on `ClientConnectorError` / `ReadTimeout` (or gets HTTP 404 from whatever now listens on that address) until the group's timeout or a manual cancel. The serve job itself is fine; only the client is stale.

Observed in marin #9920 and #9984 on cw-rno2a, 2026-10-09/10: nine evaluation groups lost this way (examples: `/karan/eval-20261009-030945-gate-rs-sft-lr1e-06-step375-5e80`, serve child `inference-553ee1e1…` preempted 6× and re-registered on 10.168.194.211 at 04:25 UTC while the eval kept 10.168.192.27:10241; `/karan/eval-20261010-030426-gate-merge-ta-a1.0-b1.0-gpqa28k-152a`, 188 logged requests answered 404 by the old address). Each costs the serve's partial GPU time plus a full relaunch; several evals ran 16–20 h before being noticed.

Expected: the client re-resolves the endpoint from the Iris registry when requests fail with connection errors (and periodically), and fails fast with a clear error when the serve job reaches a terminal state instead of retrying forever.

Done when: an eval whose serve is preempted and re-registered elsewhere continues against the new address, and an eval whose serve job dies fails within a bounded time with the serve job's state in the error.

🤖
# Research

Evalchemy launches with direct routing, and the orchestrator resolves the serve endpoint once before putting that pod address in the child job's config. The child keeps using that address while `eval_job.wait(timeout=inf)` blocks; serve health is checked only before and after the evaluation. [PR #9480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9480) chose direct routing after 7,734 hub and 10,749 peer proxy 502s in five minutes, so the recovery path must preserve direct connection reuse.

**Relevant code**
- [`launch.py#L195`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7405c96fe6ea3675d5a1bf7977d406cfc3887243/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L195) — selects direct Evalchemy routing
- [`runner.py#L352-L363`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7405c96fe6ea3675d5a1bf7977d406cfc3887243/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L352-L363) — resolves before evaluation
- [`runner.py#L602-L609`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7405c96fe6ea3675d5a1bf7977d406cfc3887243/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L602-L609) — turns registry entry into a fixed URL
- [`evalchemy/runner.py#L223-L233`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7405c96fe6ea3675d5a1bf7977d406cfc3887243/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L223-L233) — serializes the URL into the child
- [`evalchemy/runner.py#L327`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7405c96fe6ea3675d5a1bf7977d406cfc3887243/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L327) — waits without checking serve state

# Proposed Fix

1. Pass the endpoint name and serve job IDs to the Evalchemy child. Point Evalchemy at a loopback HTTP forwarder in that child; the forwarder uses a pooled connection to the current direct Iris endpoint and preserves streaming responses.
2. Refresh the registry address periodically and immediately after connection errors, timeouts, or a 404. Replace the upstream pool when the address changes, retry requests that have not started a response, and wait through a live job's preemption; propagate a 404 from an unchanged current address.
3. Poll serve status while the parent waits for the Evalchemy job. On a terminal serve state, cancel the evaluator and record `INFRA_FAILED` with the serve job ID and state within one poll interval; update both evaluation call paths to pass the inference session.
4. Cover address replacement, a stale-address 404, streaming interruption, recovery with no registered endpoint, and terminal serve state using local HTTP servers and a fake registry. Compare request failures and latency at Evalchemy's default concurrency before replacing direct routing.

topics.title: datakit: decontam is precision-favoring — low recall on embedded/short-line contamination
topics.body:
## Description
Decontamination flags very few documents (~0.01% overall; 0% on arXiv/news). This is **not** a coverage gap and **not** a verbatim-recall failure — it is the recall cost of a deliberately precision-favoring matching design. The question for the team is whether that tradeoff is calibrated where they want it.

### What's confirmed
- Benchmark coverage is comprehensive: 600 families incl. MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, HellaSwag, GPQA, MATH, DROP, SQuAD, TriviaQA, BBH, AGIEval, …
- Verbatim contamination in a ≥13-word paragraph **is** caught (reproduced a real flagged doc at 0.867 overlap).
- By design, decon (`marin.datakit.decon`) matches 13-word n-grams per paragraph and flags at ≥50% paragraph overlap, and **intentionally ignores paragraphs with <13 words** — the whole-paragraph fallback was removed in #5656 because it produced ~18% phantom contamination from trivial stubs (`"..."`, `"A."`, `"##"`).

### Recall cost of that design (injection test — see comment below)
- **Short-line contamination escapes entirely**: the same contaminated text re-wrapped to 8-word lines → overlap 0.87 → **0.00**. Affects MMLU/ARC options, tables, poetry, any line-broken benchmark text.
- **Embedded contamination is diluted below threshold**: the same paragraph + 1× filler → 0.87 → **0.02**, because overlap is a fraction of the paragraph.

### The decision
Is ~0% flagging the intended operating point — accept missing short-line/embedded leakage in exchange for near-zero false positives — or should recall be raised at the cost of more false positives? If the latter, options that keep the `"..."` artifact suppressed: length-normalize or lower the threshold, add a short-paragraph sliding-window path with a minimum length, or flag on an absolute count of matched n-gram hits rather than the paragraph fraction.

topics.title: [grug] Run the shared experts' SwiGLU in QuACK GEMM epilogues
topics.body:
The hero's shared experts run their gate/up and down projections as QuACK GEMMs with SwiGLU and its backward in the epilogues: forward and backward of one shared expert take 13.93 ms instead of 14.51 ms at the hero's per-GPU shape (65536 tokens, width 6144, intermediate width 3072). Removing the change from all of #9708 slows the step by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs of runs.

With every PR of this stack and #9829, one 64-GPU hero rack ran 12.590 s/step (31.18% MFU), against 13.899 s (28.24% MFU) for main at #9708's base, with loss within 4.9e-4 of a run of #9708.

Each shared expert runs as two per-shard ops: a gate/up GEMM against interleaved weights with SwiGLU in its epilogue, returning the pre-activations and h, and a down op whose backward runs the SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM's epilogue. dx and the gate/up weight gradient are single GEMMs on the interleaved layout. The split keeps the gate/up projection movable, so #9835 can run the first shared expert's gate/up beside the first dispatch. The weights stay separate FSDP leaves, gathered inside the shard map, so their gradients still reduce-scatter. Without QuACK, for another activation, or for operands other than bfloat16, the same ops run as XLA einsums.

Since only the down op reads h, the gate/up op stops h's gradient; otherwise the dispatch overlap would hand back dense zeros for h and the backward would run a SwiGLU backward over [T, 2I] per layer that adds nothing. SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator. Against an fp32 reference in a 4-GPU model gate, the loss error moves from 5.1e-5 to 4.5e-5 and the shared-expert gradient error from 1.22e-2 to 1.15e-2.

Directly on #9835 the change measured -0.11% (12.638 to 12.652 s): there the shared GEMMs cover the transports, and the shorter GEMMs left 0.24 s/step more transport exposed. Measured without #9835 it gained 0.72%, with peak HBM 123.4 to 121.9 GiB.

The QuACK availability check moves to `levanter.grug._moe.availability` and asks the default device for its platform. The shared experts' kernel selection calls it outside the ragged backend, where a test that stubs `jax.default_backend` on CPU devices would make the old check's `jax.devices("gpu")` raise.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [haliax] Prefer XLA ragged_dot on AMD MI300X and MI325X
topics.body:
On AMD MI300X and MI325X (gfx942), `ragged_dot(implementation="auto")` now tries XLA before the Pallas Triton kernels. MI350X (gfx950), NVIDIA, TPU and CPU keep their current order. `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` still overrides the choice.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X found that XLA's bf16 grouped GEMM takes 11-28% less time than the best Triton config for each fwd, dlhs and drhs triple. For example, the June w13 projection at M=131072 took 10.91 ms with XLA and 12.25 ms with tuned Triton. These numbers come from microbenchmarks only. We have not run a full-model A/B on MI300X. MI350X must keep Triton because XLA rejects bf16 `ragged_dot` on gfx950.

XLA's hipBLASLt grouped GEMM crashes with `ROCM_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` when HIP command buffers are on, so ROCm runs must pass `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`. The MI300X timings above used that flag. The Grug training entry points already set it by default, and so does the HPC Fund Slurm wrapper, `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` on `main`.

`_GpuFamily` gains an `AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` member, detected from the compute capability that ROCm reports (`"gfx942"`). gfx942 keeps the tile-map kernels and the block configs swept on MI350X, so the Triton fallback is unchanged. #9905 is stacked on this PR and reuses `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` for its MI300X block configs, so merge #10009, then this PR, then #9905.

At #9905's head, which contains this PR, the file gives 46 passed and 30 skipped f32 kernel cases on MI300X (job 458222) and 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223).

topics.title: [datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
topics.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores: one
Zephyr task per normalized shard on GPU workers, tokenizing the text through the
tokenize stage's own core and reading the Harrier embedding by position. The Nemotron
tokenize leaves the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's
scores are registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than
rescored; a rerun of the score stage lands at the step's own identity. The
content-type leaves written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard, so a leaf from a
different normalize run fails its shard. `QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is
removed; the stage report reads its spot-check text from the normalized shard of
the same basename.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `QualityPin` carries
separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file, checked by the
worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed dataset without
moving or rescoring the raw scores. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to identical
weights and scores, and the calibration file parses into a `Calibration`
dataclass.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage run from text against the
same embeddings matched the pinned scores to a maximum difference of 1.6e-3 (mean
2.3e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a 4,096-document batch against the
earlier 32,768.
