topics.title: [grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch
topics.body:
The scaling-ladder launcher takes --seq-len and holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, and gate/router weight decay therefore match the 4K run. A changed context requires an explicit --qk-mult, applied to all attention layers; --capacity-factor overrides the expert receiver capacity. A resume at a new context also requires --context-switch-step and --flops-baseline-step/--flops-baseline-total. The new prior_context_phases argument of harrier_mix_2026_08_18_data_config turns the switch step into LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases, with the Harrier stage schedule at the 4K batch size and the 4K shuffle blocks, so the Harrier sources continue from their 4K reads. Hero eval stays at 4K packing. A context switch is rejected for runs below the 1e23-FLOP simulated-epoching cutoff, because the data offsets assume each source reads its whole cache.

trigger_hero.sh records the context, batch, QK multiplier, capacity, eval context, FLOPs baseline, and context switch step in the W&B lineage and the #8506 launch record.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh still launches at 4K. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

Stacked on #9890, which is stacked on #9888. Part of #9615

topics.title: [marin] Keep Kueue-gated serve tasks in the placement budget
topics.body:
Iris reports a Pending pod as BUILDING, including a pod that Kueue still holds at its admission gate (status message `SchedulingGated: ...`). The eval runner's endpoint wait in `marin.inference.iris` counted BUILDING as placed, so the 2,400 s startup budget ran while the serve job was still queued for GPUs. Eight eval groups failed this way in one night with no GPU allocated.

A BUILDING task whose status message starts with `SchedulingGated` now counts as queued. The 4 h placement budget covers gated time, and the startup budget starts only once the gate is lifted. A preemption requeue still resets the startup budget. The wait now reads per-task status with `list_tasks` because the job-level state counts do not carry the status message.

A pod that Kueue has admitted but the scheduler reports `Unschedulable` still counts as placed, so the startup budget bounds an admitted pod that does not start. `Unschedulable` can mean a bad resource request or ordinary capacity or affinity limits; this keeps the existing behavior for both.

Separate from #10030 / #10033.

Fixes #10036

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run, one ContextPhaseConfig per length. With prior_context_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. So is a phase at the same sequence length as the one before it, since there a source could continue in place and the skip would only discard data. The seed, the source order, and restoring at the last switch step cannot be checked from the config, so the field docstring states them. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

Part of #9615

topics.title: [grug] Select the hero router's top-k experts with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
The hero router's top-(K+1) expert selection runs in a Triton kernel instead of a full XLA sort of every row: 0.096 ms per call instead of 0.856 ms at [65536, 384], k = 9 on one GB200, once in the forward and again in the recompute. The indices and their order match `jax.lax.top_k` bitwise for every input, including ties, signed zeros, infinities and NaNs.

XLA:GPU uses its own top-k kernel only for rows of at least 1,024 elements, so 384-expert rows fall back to a sort. The new kernel takes float32 rows narrower than 1,024 on a GPU device; everything else keeps `jax.lax.top_k`. Its gate asks the default device whether it is a GPU, because a hero test stubs `jax.default_backend` to trace a GPU-only path on CPU devices. The Triton gather-sum's gate makes the same check.

One warp holds one row in registers, as one power-of-two tile or, when that pads less, three equal ones (a 384-wide row is three 128-wide tiles), and takes k successive maxima over XLA's float32 total-order key, breaking ties by the lower column. A row in one warp keeps both reductions inside the warp; Triton reduces across warps through shared memory. A taken or absent entry gets the smallest key and the column n, which the lowest-column reduction never returns, so a negative NaN with payload 0xFFFFFFFF, whose key is also the smallest, is not mistaken for one. The kernel reads an int32 view of the input, so autodiff never asks it for a JVP rule. For k above 16 the steps run in a loop, which compiles in 0.2 s where unrolled steps take 36 s at k = 384.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that took 0.125 ms per call shortened the step by 0.53%.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [Post-training][Model merging] Initial Experiments in Model Merging with Snowball 67B A2B
topics.body:
We implemented eleven model-merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 Snowball 67B A2B checkpoint variants with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores. Sequential merging via selective expert transfer retained almost all of the NUPA source's performance and matched the BFCL source's score, but the three best merges retained essentially none of the Base model's routed experts. We have not yet run the complete cohort of policy evals needed to judge non-targeted performance.

[Earlier RLVR experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735) showed that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can strongly and unpredictably affect non-targeted benchmarks. It can introduce or repair behavioral defects that change scores while leaving the model's underlying “knowledge” essentially untouched. For example, a model might return every numeric answer, such as “31.7,” as “final_answer.31.7” instead of the requested “Final Answer: 31.7,” collapsing a benchmark score. We conservatively treat these as model defects to remedy under normal use conditions rather than grader defects to smooth. Each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats, so we investigated efficient ways to combine checkpoints.

Model merging is popular among hobbyists and is rumored to be used extensively at frontier labs, though the scientific literature is thin. Most merging methods use very few FLOPs and often require no GPUs. This makes merging relevant to our goal of reaching the frontier quickly and FLOP-efficiently.

The target Snowball checkpoint had largely improved but acquired two severe behavioral defects that sharply reduced NUPA and BFCL performance. We used two other Snowball models as merge sources. Each was an expert on one target benchmark, but both were generally inferior to the target, or Base, model. The objective was to raise performance on both disparate target benchmarks without degrading non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all standard merging approaches we tried failed to raise both target scores strongly. They restored capability weakly on both benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. Extensive experimentation led us to try sequential merging via selective expert transfer. It retained performance on both targets, but required discarding essentially all Base parameters from the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

These three merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched the source BFCL score. None appears to meet the objective of avoiding degradation on non-targeted benchmarks; we will reserve judgment until the complete policy eval cohort has run.

Sequential merging via selective expert transfer appears promising for complex MoE merges. Our best strategy combined weights from the NUPA, BFCL, and Base models:

1. Start with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template.
2. Replace selected NUPA routed experts with BFCL experts. In each layer, select 32 expert positions using BFCL activation measurements and copy BFCL weights into them. This discards all Base routed experts.
3. Change NUPA's shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We made three versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

The percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version had the highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model:

- Starting with BFCL, copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts yielded only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA, copying 32 BFCL-selected experts yielded 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor, the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We found no better joint result with those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights, and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce. This was likely an unusually difficult merge target because tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently:

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA's tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base's tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers. This affects benchmarks even with unchanged weights: the same input text can produce different token IDs, and the same output token ID can decode to different text. The numerical vocabulary did not change. Both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

The chat templates also formatted tool use differently:

- NUPA's template presents tool definitions as one JSON array; Base's presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA's template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided; Base's omits those IDs.
- The templates differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Using the other template changes the model input and therefore the benchmarks. In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input:

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA's own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

The agent's experimental design was flawed and needs a follow-up study. It drifted almost immediately from adding specialist capabilities to Base toward combining the two specialists. We will enforce that specialist changes target only a small, measured fraction of Base weights in the follow-up study, and may also control for the tokenizer confound.

---

## Campaign 2: preserve Base while importing specialist capabilities

TL;DR: We completed 48 additional merges across 12 method families (four variants each), requiring at least 75% of original Base scalar weights and every non-weight model file to remain unchanged. DARE-TIES-02 gave the best observed BFCL + NUPA sum, **45.53**, while changing **6.04%** of Base parameters. Its score was BFCL **45.53%**, NUPA200 **0.00%**; the fresh Base control scored **9.76% / 0.00%** respectively. We improved tool-use performance under the constraint, but did not recover strong performance on both targets together.

[Best checkpoint on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10/tree/153f5369f69a0c0a7203779099ec94e98c66748f) · [Implementation PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) · [Reproduction README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/README.md) · [Complete tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/TRACKER.md) · [Unrounded scores, coverage and timings](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/results-evidence.json)

NUPA200 tests numerical understanding and arithmetic across number representations, using a fixed 200-item subset of the policy’s 5,000-item set and the pinned loose-format extraction plus exact-match rule. BFCL-Parity uses the 123-trial Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent; its verified solve rate is not the full BFCL leaderboard score.

Base is Grug Antidoom Step12; the NUPA donor is Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92, and the BFCL donor is Grug Reference-KL Step20. The README pins all three revisions. This extends the first campaign's 11 families with ISO-Merger and applies the changed-weight constraint to every family. All 48 construction audits passed; actual changed scalar counts range from **3.02% to 23.50%**. The 25% rule is measured against original Base, including both serial stages; blends count as changed wherever stored bits differ. These constraints do not establish non-target capability retention, which was not evaluated for this cohort.

What worked: DARE-TIES-02 had the highest observed summed target score, with 6.04% of Base parameters changed. DARE-TIES-03 scored 41.46 with 8.34% changed; ISO-03 scored 44.09 with 23.14% changed. DARE-TIES-02 is better on both objectives than either of those alternatives. DARE-linear-02 scored 36.27 with effectively the same changed count as DARE-TIES-02 (14 fewer scalar parameters among about 4.05 billion). Thus the ranking is not just a reward for modifying a larger fraction of Base.

What did not transfer well: learned coefficients, curvature grafting and activation-selected expert transfers did not beat the best DARE-TIES candidate on the summed target metric. Activation-02 had the highest observed NUPA200 score, **10.00%**, but BFCL fell to **5.69%**. The byte-identical serial-02 control scored **7.00% / 5.69%**, showing repeat-run variation. The summed objective also permits a winner with zero NUPA; it does not require balanced capability recovery.

Why remains uncertain. Zero-score trace reviews found both arithmetic errors and correct final numbers accompanied by commentary that failed the fixed response-format rule. Weight changes can affect both capability and response behavior; this study does not isolate their causal contributions. Expert Merging++ and OTA+FFG are native-MoE adaptations trained on 48 independent synthetic calibration examples, and ISO operates on selected expert matrices. Their negative results do not establish that the original methods fail generally. NUPA's exact common ancestor with Base remains unestablished despite aligned tensor coordinates.

All 96 target evaluations are complete under the pinned evaluation policy. These are single-run search results, not statistically resolved method rankings. The campaign is sealed; no further OOD evaluations are planned. The README includes regeneration commands and states the remaining exact-replay gaps: historical calibration tensors and raw evaluation transcripts remain in private storage.

{"body":"🤖 **Config change: KDA write and erase gates dropped** (Gated DeltaNet-2 gates, adopted in batch 88)

They were worth −0.0024 at d512 (batch 88, two seeds) for about +1% step time. At the hero shape, d6144 / 48 layers on one GB200 rack, they cost far more: each is a full 6144×6144 projection in all 36 KDA layers.

| GB200 1-rack, late steps | step time | MFU | tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| with write + erase gates | 19.42 s | 25.7% | 216k |
| without (`lc1-gb200-nogate30`) | **17.95 s** | **27.6%** | **232k** |

Kimi K3's KDA has neither gate: it keeps a full-rank output gate, a low-rank decay gate and a per-head β ([arXiv 2607.24653](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1)). The base config is now `base16` (base15 without `kda_write_gate`, `kda_erase_gate`, `kda_onchip_erase_gate`), and new d512 pairs run against it.
